name: Classic-Style Test 6
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: Glaciologist: The Vellin Glacier has retreated nearly two kilometers over the past century, and many visitors assume that the retreat began with the warming of recent decades. But survey markers left by mapmakers in the 1880s show that the glacier’s front was already pulling back then, long before that warming started. So recent warming cannot be the whole explanation for the glacier’s retreat, even if it has sped the retreat up.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the glaciologist’s argument?
choices: The Vellin Glacier has retreated nearly two kilometers over the past century.
Recent warming does not by itself account for the retreat of the Vellin Glacier.
Recent warming has increased the rate at which the Vellin Glacier is retreating.
The front of the Vellin Glacier was already pulling back in the 1880s.
Visitors are mistaken in believing that the Vellin Glacier is retreating.
questions.explanation: The word “So” introduces the point everything else supports: recent warming cannot be the whole explanation for the retreat, which (B) restates. (C) is tempting, but the glaciologist only concedes that warming may have sped things up (“even if”); that is not asserted, let alone argued for. (D) is the evidence, and (E) distorts the visitors’ view, which is about when the retreat began, not whether it is happening.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Recent warming cannot be the whole explanation for the Vellin Glacier’s retreat.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Mapmakers’ markers show the front was already pulling back in the 1880s, before recent warming started.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The first sentence is background: the glacier retreated and visitors blame recent warming. The 1880s markers are the evidence. “So” flags the point: warming isn’t the whole story. It’s like saying: the leak started before the new tenant moved in, so the new tenant can’t be the whole reason the ceiling is damaged. The “even if” clause is a concession, not a claim the speaker argues for.

choices.note: Background. It sets the scene and nobody disputes it. Nothing in the argument is offered to prove it.
CORRECT. “Cannot be the whole explanation” means the same thing as “does not by itself account for.” It’s what “So” introduces, and the 1880s evidence is there to support it.

Tempting, because it appears in the last sentence. But read the words: “even if it has sped the retreat up.” The glaciologist allows that this might be true without asserting it. A concession isn’t the conclusion.
This is the premise. The survey markers prove it, and it in turn proves the conclusion. It sits in the middle of the support structure, not at the top.
Distortion. The visitors think the glacier is retreating, and the glaciologist agrees. The disagreement is about when the retreat began and what caused it.

questions.stimulus: Blogger: Sleep researchers insist that adults who regularly sleep fewer than six hours a night are at increased risk of serious illness. But my grandfather slept about five hours a night for his entire adult life and was rarely sick a day before he died at ninety-one. Clearly, the researchers have overstated the dangers of short sleep.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the blogger’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: takes for granted that what is true of most adults must also be true of elderly adults
fails to specify how many hours of sleep would be enough to avoid an increased risk of illness
presumes, without providing justification, that the researchers’ findings were based on a small sample
treats a single case as sufficient to show that a claim about increased risk across a population is exaggerated
relies on the account of a person who has no expertise in sleep research
questions.explanation: A claim about increased risk is a claim about how often illness occurs across many short sleepers, so one healthy short sleeper is fully compatible with it; (D) names this. (E) is tempting, but the blogger isn’t relying on anyone’s expert opinion, just on one case, and an expert reporting the same single case would make the same mistake.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Sleep researchers have overstated the dangers of short sleep.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The blogger’s grandfather slept about five hours a night, was rarely sick, and lived to ninety-one.

breakdown.analysis: So what if Grandpa was fine? “Increased risk” means more illness across a big group, not illness for every member. One lucky person doesn’t touch that. This is the anecdote-versus-general-claim flaw; it’s a classic, know it. It’s like saying seatbelts are overrated because your neighbor never wore one and never got hurt. We need an answer that says the blogger uses one case to knock down a claim about risk.

choices.note: The blogger never moves from most adults to elderly adults. The researchers’ claim is about adults generally, and the grandfather was one. Wrong flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most adults need about eight hours of sleep, so my eighty-year-old aunt must need eight hours too.

choices.note: So? The argument doesn’t need an exact threshold. The problem is the evidence, not a missing number.
The blogger says nothing about the researchers’ sample. If anything, the blogger is the one with the tiny sample.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The researchers must have studied only a handful of people, so their warning can be ignored.

choices.note: CORRECT. The whole case is one person. A claim about risk across a population allows for plenty of healthy exceptions, so one exception can’t show the risk is overstated.

Tempting, because the grandfather isn’t a scientist. But the argument doesn’t rest on his expertise or opinion; it rests on what happened to him. Even if a sleep researcher reported the same single case, it still wouldn’t show the risk is exaggerated.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: My dentist says this stock is a great investment, so it must be.

questions.stimulus: Last year the health department of Corrin ran a campaign urging residents over forty to have their blood pressure checked. During the following year, the number of Corrin residents being treated for high blood pressure rose by a third, even though there is no evidence that residents’ diets, weight, or exercise habits changed during that period.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the rise in the number of Corrin residents being treated for high blood pressure?
choices: Many Corrin residents who already had high blood pressure before the campaign had not known that they had it.
High blood pressure is considerably more common among people over forty than among younger people.
The campaign’s advertisements also urged residents to reduce the amount of salt in their diets.
In a neighboring city that ran no such campaign, the number of residents treated for high blood pressure stayed about the same.
Some of the residents who had their blood pressure checked as a result of the campaign learned that it was normal.
questions.explanation: If many residents already had undiagnosed high blood pressure, the screening campaign would bring them into treatment without any change in the underlying condition, which is (A). (D) is tempting because it ties the rise to the campaign, but it only shows that the campaign made a difference; it doesn’t say how a checkup campaign could raise treatment numbers when health habits stayed the same.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Residents’ habits didn’t change, but after a screening campaign the number being treated for high blood pressure jumped by a third.

breakdown.analysis: How can more people be treated if nobody got less healthy? Easy: they were already sick and nobody knew. A campaign that gets people checked finds cases that were there all along. It’s like a new smoke detector “causing” more fire alarms: the smoke was already there, now somebody is noticing it. We need an answer that says there were hidden cases waiting to be found.

choices.note: CORRECT. If lots of residents had high blood pressure without knowing it, a campaign that gets them checked would diagnose them and put them into treatment. More treatment, same health habits. That’s the whole puzzle solved.
So? This was true before and after the campaign. A constant fact can’t explain a change. It also doesn’t explain why the targeted group suddenly showed up for treatment.
This pushes the wrong way. Less salt would tend to lower blood pressure, so if anything it makes the rise more puzzling.

Tempting, because it points to the campaign as the cause. But the puzzle is how a checkup campaign could raise treatment numbers when nothing about health changed. This shows the campaign mattered; it doesn’t show how.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. People with normal readings wouldn’t be treated, so they don’t help explain more treatment.

questions.stimulus:
Imre: When translating a poem, a translator should preserve the original’s meter and rhyme even when doing so requires loosening its literal meaning. A poem’s sound is part of what the poem says.

Dana: People read a translated poem to learn what the poem says. A translator who sacrifices literal meaning for the sake of rhyme gives readers lines that the original poet never wrote.
questions.stem: Imre and Dana disagree over whether
choices: it is possible to preserve a poem’s meter and rhyme in translation
most readers of translated poetry know the language in which the poem was originally written
a translator of poetry should loosen a poem’s literal meaning in order to preserve its rhyme
a poem’s sound is the most important part of what the poem says
translators of poetry often find it difficult to preserve a poem’s literal meaning
questions.explanation: Imre says a translator should loosen literal meaning to keep meter and rhyme; Dana objects that doing so gives readers lines the poet never wrote, so they disagree about (C). (D) is tempting, but Imre says only that sound is part of what a poem says, not the most important part, so Imre isn’t committed to it.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Imre: Keep meter and rhyme even at the cost of literal meaning, because sound is part of what a poem says.; Dana: Readers want to know what the poem says, so trading meaning for rhyme gives them lines the poet never wrote.

breakdown.analysis: What is Imre recommending, and what is Dana attacking? The same thing: trading literal meaning for rhyme. Imre says do it; Dana says it shortchanges readers. To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. We need an answer about whether a translator should give up literal meaning to keep the rhyme.

choices.note: Neither speaker doubts that it can be done. Imre assumes it’s possible, and Dana objects to the cost, not the feasibility. No disagreement.
Neither speaker mentions what readers know. Dana talks about why people read translations, but that’s different.
CORRECT. Imre: yes, loosen the meaning to keep meter and rhyme. Dana: no, that gives readers words the poet never wrote. One yes, one no.

Tempting, because Imre values sound. But Imre says sound is “part of” what a poem says, not the most important part. Imre isn’t committed to this, so it can’t be the point at issue. Watch the jump from “part” to “most.”
Neither speaker addresses how often translators struggle. Both might agree it’s often hard; that’s not what they’re fighting about.

questions.stimulus: Bookshop owner: Since the café next door closed in March, our weekday afternoon sales have dropped by a quarter. Many of our afternoon customers used to stop in to browse after leaving the café. So if a new café opens in that space, our afternoon sales will probably recover.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the bookshop owner’s argument?
choices: The café that closed in March was the most popular café in the neighborhood.
Most of the bookshop’s afternoon customers before March had come to the shop directly from the café next door.
A new café is likely to open in the space next door within the next year.
The bookshop’s afternoon sales before March were higher than in any previous year.
A new café next door would draw at least some customers who would also stop in to browse at the bookshop.
questions.explanation: The prediction depends on a new café bringing back the browsing traffic, so the owner must assume that a new café would draw at least some customers who would stop in at the bookshop (E); negate it and recovery has no mechanism. (B) is tempting, but the owner says only that “many” customers came from the café, and sales could recover even if fewer than half did.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If a new café opens next door, the bookshop’s afternoon sales will probably recover.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Afternoon sales fell by a quarter after the café closed; many afternoon customers used to browse after leaving the café.

breakdown.analysis: Why would a new café help? Only if its customers also wander into the bookshop. The old café sent browsers over, but a new one might draw a totally different crowd: commuters grabbing coffee to go, say. The owner needs at least some of the new café’s customers to stop in. Test each choice by negating it: if the negation kills the argument, it’s required.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The old café didn’t need to be the most popular for its customers to matter to the bookshop. Negate it and nothing changes.
choices.negation: The café that closed in March was not the most popular café in the neighborhood.

choices.note: Tempting, because it fits the story. But the owner says “many,” not “most.” Negate it: maybe only 30 percent came from the café. A new café could still bring those people back. The argument survives, so this isn’t required.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most of the bookshop’s afternoon customers before March had come from the café.

choices.note: The conclusion is conditional: “if a new café opens.” The owner doesn’t predict that one will open. Negating this doesn’t hurt the if-then claim.
choices.negation: A new café is not likely to open in the space next door within the next year.

choices.note: Irrelevant. How pre-March sales compared with earlier years doesn’t bear on whether a new café would restore them. Negation does nothing.
choices.negation: The bookshop’s afternoon sales before March were not higher than in every previous year.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: a new café would attract no one who would stop in at the bookshop. Then a new café can’t bring sales back, and the conclusion collapses. Notice the modest wording, “at least some”; that’s typical of a right answer here.
choices.negation: A new café next door would draw no customers who would also stop in to browse at the bookshop.

questions.stimulus: Entomologist: Males of the leaf beetle Calopha virens have unusually long antennae, nearly twice the length of the females’. In many insect species, males locate mates by detecting airborne chemicals released by females. So the long antennae of male C. virens probably serve mainly to help them find mates.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the entomologist’s argument?
choices: Male C. virens use their antennae chiefly to fence with rival males over feeding sites.
Female C. virens release airborne chemicals that males can detect from several meters away.
In some other species of leaf beetle, the females have longer antennae than the males.
Male C. virens whose antennae have been damaged are less likely to mate than males whose antennae are intact.
The antennae of C. virens contain a large number of sensory cells.
questions.explanation: The argument guesses the antennae’s function from what is true of other insects; (A) offers a different function, fencing with rivals over feeding sites, which undercuts the inference that their main use is finding mates. (D) may look like a weakener but it is consistent with the entomologist’s view, and (B) actually supports it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Male C. virens’ long antennae probably serve mainly to help them find mates.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The males’ antennae are nearly twice as long as the females’; in many insect species, males find mates by sensing females’ airborne chemicals.

breakdown.analysis: Just because many insects use antennae to sniff out mates, does that mean this beetle does? Maybe its antennae do something else. This is a function guess, and the classic way to weaken a function guess is to show a different job the trait actually does. We need an answer that gives the long antennae another main use.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the males mainly use their antennae as weapons against rival males over feeding sites, then their main use isn’t finding mates. A plausible alternative function weakens the guess.
This helps the entomologist. If females give off chemicals males can detect, sensing mates with antennae looks even more likely.
Other species are a different group. What females of other beetles have doesn’t tell us what this male’s antennae are for.
Tempting if you read it fast, but it fits the entomologist’s view: damaged antennae, fewer matings. At most it’s neutral, since damage could matter for other reasons too.
So? Lots of sensory cells is consistent with sensing mates. It doesn’t point to any other function.

questions.stimulus: Researchers asked mock jurors to read a trial transcript and decide whether the defendant was guilty. Half of the jurors read a version in which the defense lawyer described the evidence in vivid, concrete language; the other half read a version that was identical except that the same evidence was described in dry, abstract terms. Jurors who read the vivid version were significantly more likely to find the defendant not guilty.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Defense lawyers who use vivid language win most of the cases they try.
Jurors pay closer attention to defense lawyers than to prosecutors.
How evidence is described, and not only what the evidence is, can influence mock jurors’ verdicts.
Describing evidence in abstract terms leads jurors to overestimate the strength of that evidence.
Mock jurors who read the vivid version understood the evidence better than those who read the dry version.
questions.explanation: The two groups saw the same evidence and differed only in how it was described, yet reached different verdicts, so the description itself can affect mock jurors’ verdicts (C). (E) is tempting as an explanation of the result, but the study measured verdicts, not understanding, and the vivid version could have swayed jurors without making the evidence clearer.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Two groups of mock jurors read the same transcript and saw the same evidence; 2. The only difference was vivid versus dry wording by the defense lawyer; 3. The vivid group acquitted significantly more often.

breakdown.analysis: Same evidence, different words, different verdicts. What does that show? That the wording matters, at least for mock jurors. That’s about all. It’s like two identical used cars, one described as “cozy and road-ready” and one as “compact, functional”: if people pay more for the first, the description did something. Watch for answers that guess at why the wording mattered, or that stretch to real trials, all lawyers, or all cases.

choices.note: Too strong. The study shows vivid wording raised the acquittal rate among mock jurors. It says nothing about real lawyers winning most of their cases.
Prosecutors aren’t in the study. Unsupported comparison.
CORRECT. The evidence was held fixed and only the description changed, and the verdicts changed. That’s exactly what this says, with the modest “can influence.”

We don’t know which version led to a more accurate judgment. Maybe the dry version produced the right reading and the vivid version led jurors to underrate the evidence. “Overestimate” assumes a fact we don’t have.
Tempting, because it offers a reason for the result. But the study measured verdicts, not understanding. Vivid language could sway people without clarifying anything. Merely possible.

questions.stimulus: Commentator: The Bramley Health Council has launched a campaign urging residents to cut back on sugary drinks. Yet several members of the council were photographed drinking soda at the campaign’s own kickoff event. Residents can therefore safely disregard the campaign’s warnings about sugary drinks.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the commentator’s argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: fails to consider that the photographs of the council members may have been misleading
rejects a recommendation on the grounds that those who make it do not follow it themselves
presumes that a campaign aimed at all residents must be appropriate for each individual resident
takes for granted that sugary drinks are no more harmful than other kinds of drinks
relies on the claims of a source that has an interest in the outcome of the campaign
questions.explanation: Whether council members drink soda has no bearing on whether sugary drinks are harmful; the commentator dismisses advice because its givers don’t follow it, which is (B). (A) is tempting, but even if the photos are perfectly accurate the conclusion still doesn’t follow, so the possibility that they mislead isn’t the argument’s real problem.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Residents can safely disregard the campaign’s warnings about sugary drinks.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Council members were photographed drinking soda at the campaign’s kickoff.

breakdown.analysis: So what if the council members drink soda? Sugar is just as bad for you whether or not the people warning you follow their own advice. This is ad hominem in its “you do it too” form (tu quoque). It’s a classic; know it. It’s like ignoring your doctor’s advice to quit smoking because she smokes. We need an answer that says the argument dismisses advice because its sources don’t follow it.

choices.note: Tempting, because it offers a way out for the council. But assume the photos are perfectly accurate: the members really drank soda. The conclusion still doesn’t follow. The flaw is in what the photos are used to prove, not whether they’re accurate.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: A photo shows the senator at the protest, so she must support the protesters’ cause.

choices.note: CORRECT. The only reason given for ignoring the warnings is that the people giving them don’t follow them. Whether sugary drinks are harmful doesn’t depend on how the council behaves.
The argument never moves from the campaign to individual residents. Wrong flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The campaign is meant for the whole town, so every resident, including marathon runners, must cut back on sugar.

choices.note: The commentator never makes a claim about how harmful sugar is compared with other drinks. The conclusion is about ignoring the warnings, and the flaw is the reason given for that.
This reverses the roles. The commentator doesn’t rely on the council’s claims; the commentator rejects them. Wrong flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The soda company’s study says soda is harmless, so we can drink as much as we like.

questions.stimulus: A museum should return an object in its collection to a community that claims it whenever the community can document that the object was removed without the community’s consent, unless returning the object would expose it to a serious risk of destruction.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: The Ferrow Museum should return a carved mask to the village of Ostel, since the villagers sincerely believe that the mask was taken from them without their consent.
The Danto Museum should not return a set of drums claimed by the Marrin community, since the drums are among the museum’s most visited exhibits.
The Lisle Museum should return a manuscript claimed by the Tavi community, since returning it would pose no risk to the manuscript.
The Graye Museum should return a textile to the Senn community, which documented that it was taken without consent, even though the community has no way to protect it from rapid decay.
The Kell Museum should return a ceremonial bowl to the Avar community, which has documented that the bowl was removed without consent and has a secure, climate-controlled building ready to house it.
questions.explanation: The principle requires documented removal without consent and no serious risk of destruction; (E) meets both, since the Avar community has documentation and a secure building. (D) is tempting because it has the documentation, but the textile would face rapid decay, which triggers the principle’s exception.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Documented removal without consent AND NOT serious risk of destruction → return the object.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: The right answer must say “return” and show 1. documentation that the object was taken without consent and 2. no serious risk of destruction if returned.

breakdown.analysis: What does a community need to get an object back? Proof, not just a belief, that it was taken without consent. And even with proof, the museum keeps the object if returning it would put it in serious danger. We need an answer that checks both boxes and then concludes the object should be returned.

choices.note: Sincere belief isn’t documentation. The first condition is unknown, so the principle doesn’t support returning the mask.
Popularity isn’t part of the principle. And the principle never tells a museum not to return something; it only says when it should. We also don’t know whether the Marrin community has documentation.
Half-right. There’s no risk, but we’re never told the Tavi community documented that the manuscript was taken without consent. Missing condition.
Tempting, because the documentation is there. But rapid decay is a serious risk of destruction, which is exactly the exception. The principle says don’t return it.
CORRECT. Documented removal without consent: check. A secure, climate-controlled building means no serious risk of destruction: check. So the principle says return it, and that’s the judgment.

questions.stimulus: Legal analyst: Under the rules of the Morvan appellate court, any appeal that raises a constitutional question must be heard by the full court rather than by a three-judge panel. The appeal in the Tessaly case has been assigned to a three-judge panel. Hence, the Tessaly appeal does not challenge the validity of a statute.
questions.stem: The legal analyst’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every appeal that does not raise a constitutional question is heard by a three-judge panel.
Some appeals that challenge the validity of a statute are heard by the full court.
Any appeal heard by the full court raises a constitutional question.
Every appeal that challenges the validity of a statute raises a constitutional question.
Appeals that raise a constitutional question are rarely assigned to a three-judge panel.
questions.explanation: Constitutional question → full court, so the Tessaly appeal, assigned to a panel, raises no constitutional question; adding (D), challenges a statute → constitutional question, lets the contrapositive finish the chain: no constitutional question → no challenge to a statute. (C) is the attractive reversal: it tells us what full-court appeals have, not what panel appeals lack.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Tessaly appeal does not challenge the validity of a statute.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Constitutional question → heard by the full court; the Tessaly appeal is heard by a three-judge panel, not the full court.

breakdown.analysis: The premises get us partway: Constitutional question → full court. Tessaly isn’t before the full court, so by contrapositive, Tessaly raises no constitutional question. But the conclusion is about challenging a statute, a term that appears nowhere in the premises. We need the bridge: challenges a statute → constitutional question. Then: Tessaly → no constitutional question → no challenge to a statute. The new term always has to be linked to the old one.

choices.note: This is about appeals without constitutional questions and where they go. It doesn’t mention statutes, so it can’t connect to the conclusion.
“Some” is too weak to prove anything about the Tessaly appeal, and it tells us about the full court, not the panel.

Tempting, because it links the full court and constitutional questions. But it reverses the premise’s direction and still leaves statutes out. Even with it, the Tessaly appeal could challenge a statute without raising a constitutional question.

CORRECT. Challenges a statute → constitutional question → full court. Contrapositive: not full court → no constitutional question → no challenge to a statute. Tessaly is before a panel, so the conclusion follows.
“Rarely” leaves room for exceptions, and it adds nothing the premises didn’t already say. It still never links constitutional questions to statutes.

questions.stimulus: Sleep researcher: In our study, office workers who kept their phones outside the bedroom for a month reported falling asleep faster, on average, than they had in the month before the study began. So keeping one’s phone out of the bedroom helps people fall asleep faster.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the sleep researcher’s argument?
choices: Some of the workers in the study said that they found it inconvenient to keep their phones outside the bedroom at night.
Office workers tend to sleep fewer hours per night than do workers in most other occupations.
Similar office workers who kept their phones in the bedroom that same month reported no change in how quickly they fell asleep.
Several of the workers in the study also reported waking up less often during the night.
The month of the study was one in which the hours of daylight were growing shorter.
questions.explanation: The before-and-after comparison leaves open that something else about that month made people fall asleep faster; (C) shows similar workers who kept their phones nearby in the same month saw no change, which rules that out. (D) is tempting but concerns a different outcome, waking during the night, not falling asleep, and (E) suggests an alternative cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Keeping one’s phone out of the bedroom helps people fall asleep faster.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Workers who kept phones out of the bedroom for a month fell asleep faster than they had the month before.

breakdown.analysis: What if everyone fell asleep faster that month: cooler nights, less work stress, the novelty of being in a study? Then the phone had nothing to do with it. A before-and-after study with no comparison group can’t separate the phone from everything else that changed. We need an answer that shows people who did NOT move their phones didn’t improve.

choices.note: Interesting fact, but not relevant. Whether the rule was annoying says nothing about whether it helped people fall asleep.
So? How much office workers sleep compared with other workers doesn’t touch whether moving the phone made a difference.

CORRECT. Same kind of workers, same month, phones still in the bedroom: no change. That rules out the idea that something about the month made everyone fall asleep faster, so the phone change looks like the cause.
Tempting, because it sounds like more good news. But the conclusion is about falling asleep faster, not waking less. A different benefit doesn’t support this claim.
This hints at a different explanation, since changing daylight can affect sleep. If anything, it weakens.

questions.stimulus: Editor: Some critics hold that a translation is faithful only to the extent that it uses, wherever possible, the word in the new language that most closely matches each word of the original. But by that standard, a translation that rendered the French idiom “il pleut des cordes” word for word as “it is raining ropes” would be more faithful than one that rendered it “it is pouring.” That is plainly wrong, since readers of the literal version would not grasp what the original says. So the critics’ standard should be rejected.
questions.stem: The claim that a word-for-word rendering of the idiom would be more faithful plays which one of the following roles in the editor’s argument?
choices: It is a consequence of the critics’ standard that the editor uses to show that the standard is mistaken.
It is the main conclusion that the editor’s argument as a whole is designed to establish.
It is a premise that the critics offer in support of their standard.
It is an example offered to show that some idioms cannot be translated at all.
It is a claim that the editor accepts but argues is irrelevant to the critics’ standard.
questions.explanation: The editor derives the claim from the critics’ standard (“by that standard”) and then calls it “plainly wrong,” so the claim is an absurd consequence used to sink the standard, which is (A). (C) is tempting, but the critics never offer this claim; the editor draws it out of their view in order to reject it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The critics’ word-matching standard of faithfulness should be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: By that standard, “it is raining ropes” would count as more faithful than “it is pouring”; that result is plainly wrong, because readers wouldn’t grasp the original’s meaning.

breakdown.analysis: Does the editor believe the word-for-word version is more faithful? No: the editor calls that “plainly wrong.” It’s the absurd result the editor derives from the critics’ rule in order to sink it. The editor doesn’t believe this; it’s used to show the rule leads somewhere silly. It’s like answering “never tell a lie” by pointing out it would require telling a burglar where your kids are hiding.

choices.note: CORRECT. “By that standard” marks it as following from the critics’ view, and “that is plainly wrong” marks the editor rejecting it. A consequence used to show the standard is mistaken.
The conclusion is that the standard should be rejected, flagged by “So.” The editor doesn’t even believe the word-for-word claim, so it can’t be what the argument sets out to prove.

Tempting, because the claim comes from the critics’ standard. But the critics never offer it as a reason. The editor derives it from their view in order to attack it. A premise of theirs would support their standard, not embarrass it.
The editor shows the idiom can be translated perfectly well, as “it is pouring.” The point is about which translation is more faithful, not about untranslatable idioms.
The editor doesn’t accept the claim; it calls it plainly wrong. And far from being irrelevant, it’s the editor’s main weapon against the standard.

questions.stimulus: For its spring exhibit, the Lindqvist Gallery used wall labels that gave only each work’s title and date, and many visitors complained that the labels were uninformative. Yet visitors to that exhibit spent more time, on average, in front of each work than visitors to any of the gallery’s previous exhibits, and a larger share of them bought the exhibit catalog.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Many of the complaints about the labels came from visitors who had attended the gallery’s previous exhibits.
The catalog for the spring exhibit was priced lower than the catalogs that the gallery had produced for its previous exhibits.
Most museums provide more information on their wall labels than the Lindqvist Gallery did for the spring exhibit.
Visitors who complain about an exhibit are less likely than other visitors to return to the museum.
Visitors who found the labels unhelpful tended to look more closely at the works and to rely on the catalog for background.
questions.explanation: (E) shows how the defect produced both results: without informative labels, visitors looked longer at the works and bought the catalog to get the information the labels lacked. (B) is tempting because it explains the catalog sales, but it does nothing to explain why visitors lingered longer in front of the works.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Visitors complained that the labels were uninformative, but they spent more time per work and bought more catalogs than at any earlier exhibit.

breakdown.analysis: How could worse labels lead to more engagement? Maybe the defect helped. If the label doesn’t tell you what to think, you look harder, and if you want the backstory, you buy the book. It’s like a restaurant with a vague menu selling more of its detailed wine guide. We need an answer that explains both results: longer looking and more catalog sales.

choices.note: So? Who complained doesn’t explain why visitors stayed longer or bought more catalogs.
Tempting, because it explains the catalog sales. But it leaves the other half untouched: why would people stand longer in front of each work? Half an explanation loses to a full one.
Comparison to other museums doesn’t help. The puzzle is within this gallery: why sparse labels went with more engagement.
Irrelevant. Whether complainers come back later has nothing to do with how they behaved during this exhibit.
CORRECT. The sparse labels themselves cause both results: visitors study the works longer and buy the catalog to fill in what the labels left out. A defect that turns out to help. Paradox resolved.

questions.stimulus: Neuroscientist: In a recent study, volunteers studied a list of words before going to bed and were later woken during deep sleep and asked to recall the list. Brain scans taken just before waking showed intense activity in the hippocampus, a brain region involved in memory, in nearly every volunteer who recalled the list well. This shows that intense hippocampal activity during deep sleep helps people retain what they learned before sleeping.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the neuroscientist’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: takes for granted that all of the volunteers studied the list of words with equal effort
fails to establish whether volunteers who recalled the list poorly also showed intense hippocampal activity
presumes, without providing justification, that the hippocampus is the only brain region involved in memory
overlooks the possibility that being woken during deep sleep makes it harder to recall what one has learned
draws a conclusion about people in general from a study of volunteers who may not be representative
questions.explanation: The study reports brain activity only for good recallers; if poor recallers showed the same intense activity, that activity can’t be what distinguishes retention, so the missing comparison group is the flaw (B). (C) is tempting but the conclusion says only that hippocampal activity “helps,” which doesn’t require it to be the only region involved; (D) would lower everyone’s recall and wouldn’t explain away the link.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Intense hippocampal activity during deep sleep helps people retain what they learned before sleeping.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nearly every volunteer who recalled the list well showed intense hippocampal activity just before waking.

breakdown.analysis: What about the volunteers who recalled the list badly? If they had the same intense activity, then the activity is just what every sleeping brain does and has nothing to do with remembering. The argument looks at only one group. It’s like noting that nearly every lottery winner bought a ticket on a Tuesday, without checking when the losers bought theirs. We need an answer that points out the missing comparison: poor recallers.

choices.note: Merely possible. Unequal effort could add noise, but it doesn’t explain why good recall goes with high hippocampal activity. And the argument never assumes equal effort.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Students who used the new textbook scored higher, so the textbook works (ignoring that some students studied much harder).

choices.note: CORRECT. The data cover only good recallers. Without knowing what poor recallers’ brains were doing, we can’t tell whether intense activity has anything to do with good recall. This is the missing-comparison-group flaw.

Tempting, because it sounds like a classic overreach. But the conclusion says the activity “helps,” not that the hippocampus is the only region that matters. The argument doesn’t need that assumption.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Exercise improves mood, so people who feel down must not be exercising.

choices.note: So? If waking people up hurts recall, it hurts everyone’s recall. That doesn’t explain why good recallers had intense activity, and it doesn’t touch the conclusion.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The new test format lowered scores, so students learned less this year (ignoring that the harder format affected everyone).

choices.note: Tempting because it’s a generic study criticism. But nothing suggests these volunteers are unusual, and even a perfectly representative sample would have the real problem: no data on poor recallers.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Members of our running club love the new shoes, so most people will love them.

questions.stimulus: In Areth County, every person summoned for jury duty either appears at the courthouse on the summons date or has been granted a deferral. A deferral is granted only to a person who has submitted a written request at least ten days before the summons date. Everyone who appears at the courthouse is entered into the pool from which juries are chosen. Last month, Ruth Ellery was summoned for jury duty in Areth County, but she was not entered into the pool.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Anyone in Areth County who submits a written request at least ten days before the summons date is granted a deferral.
Ruth Ellery appeared at the courthouse but was excused from serving.
Some people in Areth County who were granted deferrals last month were entered into the pool.
Ruth Ellery submitted a written request at least ten days before her summons date.
Ruth Ellery will be summoned for jury duty again within the next year.
questions.explanation: Ruth wasn’t entered into the pool, so she didn’t appear; a summoned person who didn’t appear was granted a deferral; and a deferral requires a written request at least ten days ahead, so (D) must be true. (A) reverses the second rule: a timely request is required for a deferral, not a guarantee of one.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Summoned → appears OR granted deferral; 2. Deferral → written request at least ten days ahead; 3. Appears → entered into pool; 4. Ruth was summoned and not entered into the pool.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. Rule 3 contrapositive: not in pool → didn’t appear. So Ruth didn’t appear. Rule 1: summoned and didn’t appear → granted a deferral. Rule 2: deferral → written request at least ten days ahead. So: Ruth not in pool → didn’t appear → deferral → timely written request. Watch for answers that reverse a link, especially “only” in rule 2.

choices.note: This reverses rule 2. A timely request is necessary for a deferral, not sufficient. Requests could be denied. “Only to” introduces the necessary condition.
Contradicts the facts. Everyone who appears is entered into the pool, and Ruth wasn’t, so she didn’t appear.
Could be true but doesn’t have to be. Nothing says people with deferrals can’t be in the pool, but nothing says any of them are.
CORRECT. Not in pool → didn’t appear → granted a deferral → submitted a written request at least ten days early. Every link comes from a stated rule.
We don’t know this. The rules say nothing about when deferred people are summoned again.

questions.stimulus: Park official: Two years ago, Fenmark National Park closed the steepest of its three glacier-viewing trails and directed hikers to the other two. Since then, the number of injuries reported on the park’s glacier-viewing trails has fallen by 40 percent, even though the number of hikers has not declined. Clearly, closing the steep trail has made hiking to view the glacier safer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the park official’s argument?
choices: The injuries now reported on the remaining trails far more often involve serious falls requiring rescue than did the injuries on the steep trail.
The two remaining trails are longer than the steep trail was, so hikers spend more time on them.
Before the steep trail was closed, most of the injuries on the glacier-viewing trails occurred on that trail.
The steep trail offered a closer view of the glacier than either of the two trails that remain open to hikers does.
The park has added new hiking trails in its forested areas, away from the glacier, during the past two years.
questions.explanation: The official measures safety by the number of injuries, but if the injuries now occurring are much more serious, hiking may not be safer overall; (A) introduces severity and weakens the conclusion. (B) is tempting because more time on a trail sounds riskier, but injuries already fell despite that, so it doesn’t undercut the result; (C) strengthens the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Closing the steep trail has made hiking to view the glacier safer.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Reported injuries on the glacier trails fell 40 percent after the closure, while the number of hikers didn’t decline.

breakdown.analysis: Is the number of injuries really the measure of safety? Ten twisted ankles are not worse than three falls that need a helicopter rescue. The official counts injuries and ignores how bad they are. We need an answer that shows the remaining injuries are more serious, so fewer injuries doesn’t mean safer hiking.

choices.note: CORRECT. The injuries happening now are far more often serious falls needing rescue than the old ones were. Fewer injuries, but worse ones, so the trails may not be safer at all. Counts versus severity.

Tempting, because more time on a trail sounds like more risk. But the injury count already fell despite the longer trails. This doesn’t show the trails are less safe; if anything, it makes the drop more impressive.
This helps the official. If most injuries happened on the steep trail, closing it should cut injuries, just as the numbers show.
Wrong dimension: the view, not safety. A worse view doesn’t make hiking more dangerous.
So? New forest trails are away from the glacier, and the hiker numbers on the glacier trails haven’t dropped. This doesn’t explain the fall in glacier-trail injuries.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Last year the town of Wexley began requiring shops on its main street to close by 9 p.m. Over the following twelve months, three of the street’s late-night businesses closed permanently. The new rule, therefore, drove those businesses out of business.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the economist’s argument depends?
choices: The three late-night businesses were the only businesses on Wexley’s main street to close last year.
Most of the three businesses’ revenue had come from sales made after 9 p.m.
At least one of the three businesses would not have closed last year if the rule had not been adopted.
The town council adopted the rule in order to reduce late-night noise on the main street.
Businesses that close by 9 p.m. generally earn less than businesses that stay open later.
questions.explanation: To blame the rule for the closures, the economist must assume the closures wouldn’t have happened anyway; negate (C) and all three businesses would have closed regardless, so the rule drove none of them out. (B) is tempting, but it is stronger than needed: a business can be ruined by losing well under half its revenue.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The 9 p.m. closing rule drove the three late-night businesses out of business.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The rule took effect; within twelve months, three late-night businesses on the street closed permanently.

breakdown.analysis: What if those three shops were going under anyway: rent hikes, a dying lease, owners retiring? Then the rule didn’t drive them out; it just happened at the same time. Any argument that blames an action for an outcome assumes the outcome wouldn’t have happened without the action. Think of a defense lawyer saying, “It would have happened anyway.” We need the answer that shuts that defense down. Test by negation.

choices.note: Too strong. Negate it: a couple of other shops also closed. The rule could still have driven out the late-night ones. The argument survives.
choices.negation: Some business on Wexley’s main street other than the three late-night businesses also closed last year.

choices.note: Tempting, because it explains how the rule could hurt. But “most” is more than the argument needs. Negate it: say 35 percent of revenue came after 9 p.m. Losing that could easily sink a shop. The argument survives.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most of the three businesses’ revenue had come from sales made after 9 p.m.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: all three businesses would have closed last year even without the rule. Then the rule drove none of them out, and the conclusion collapses. The modest “at least one” wording is typical of a required assumption.
choices.negation: All three of the businesses would have closed last year even if the rule had not been adopted.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Why the council passed the rule has nothing to do with what the rule did to these shops.
choices.negation: The town council did not adopt the rule in order to reduce late-night noise on the main street.

choices.note: Too general and not needed. Negate it: early-closing businesses don’t generally earn less. These particular shops could still have been ruined by losing their late hours.
choices.negation: Businesses that close by 9 p.m. do not generally earn less than businesses that stay open later.

questions.stimulus: Entomologist: Every moth species that spends the winter as a pupa in the Delmar Forest has larvae that feed on oak leaves. The larvae of the ash-winged moth feed on oak leaves. So the ash-winged moth must spend the winter as a pupa in the Delmar Forest.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the entomologist’s argument?
choices: Every restaurant on Corder Street that has outdoor seating serves breakfast. The Blue Heron, a restaurant on Corder Street, does not serve breakfast. So the Blue Heron must not have outdoor seating.
Every violin made in the Pazzi workshop has a maple back. This violin was not made in the Pazzi workshop. So this violin must not have a maple back.
Most of the paintings in the Ostler collection are landscapes. This painting is in the Ostler collection. So this painting must be a landscape.
Only members of the Harlan choir may use the choir’s rehearsal hall. Tomas uses the choir’s rehearsal hall. So Tomas must be a member of the Harlan choir.

To be eligible for the Halden Prize, a novel must have been published within the past two years. Mira Ravel’s novel was published last year. So Mira Ravel’s novel must be eligible for the Halden Prize.
questions.explanation: The entomologist reasons: overwinters as pupa → oak-feeding larvae; this moth has oak-feeding larvae; so it overwinters as a pupa, treating a necessary condition as sufficient. (E) does the same once its “must” wording is translated: eligible → published recently; this novel was published recently; so it’s eligible. (D) looks like the same shape but is valid (uses the hall → member), and (B) is flawed in a different way, by negating the condition.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The ash-winged moth must overwinter as a pupa in the Delmar Forest.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Overwinters as a pupa in Delmar → larvae feed on oak; ash-winged larvae feed on oak.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are B; this is B; so this is A (treats a necessary condition as sufficient).

breakdown.analysis: Does feeding on oak prove the moth overwinters in Delmar? No. The rule only says Delmar overwinterers eat oak; plenty of oak-eaters could winter somewhere else. That’s confusing a necessary condition with a sufficient one, also called affirming the consequent. It’s a classic; know it. Translate each choice into arrows. The match has the form A → B; B; therefore A. Beware choices that use the valid contrapositive, and choices whose “only” or “must” wording hides the direction.

choices.note: Outdoor seating → breakfast; Blue Heron has no breakfast; so no outdoor seating. That’s the contrapositive, which is valid. A valid argument can’t match a flawed one.

Tempting, because it’s flawed and about a rule with “every.” But the flaw is different: Pazzi → maple; not Pazzi; so not maple. That negates the condition (denying the antecedent) instead of affirming the outcome.
Flawed, but in a different way: it treats “most” as “all.” There’s no conditional rule being reversed.

Tempting, because the shape looks identical: rule, a fact about Tomas, “must” conclusion. But “only members may use” means uses → member. Tomas uses the hall, so he’s a member. That’s valid. “Only” introduces the necessary condition.

CORRECT. “To be eligible, a novel must have been published within two years” means eligible → recent. Ravel’s novel is recent, so the argument concludes it’s eligible. That’s B; therefore A, the same reversal as the moth argument, disguised by the “must” wording.

questions.stimulus: Judge: During the trial, juror Pell admitted that he had searched online for the defendant’s name, though he says he found nothing about the case. Even if Pell is telling the truth, he should be removed from the jury. It is essential that the public be able to see that a verdict rests only on the evidence presented in court.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the judge’s reasoning?
choices: A juror should be removed from a jury only if the juror has actually encountered information about the case from a source outside the courtroom.
A juror whose conduct could lead the public to doubt that the verdict rests only on courtroom evidence should be removed, even if the conduct had no actual effect on the juror.
Jurors who are honest with the court about their misconduct should be treated more leniently than jurors who try to conceal it.
Any juror who lies to the court about his or her conduct during a trial should be removed from the jury.
The public’s confidence in the courts depends more on the fairness of verdicts than on their accuracy.
questions.explanation: The judge wants Pell removed even if his search turned up nothing, because the public must be able to see that verdicts rest only on courtroom evidence; (B) says exactly that conduct casting such doubt warrants removal regardless of actual influence. (D) is tempting, but the judge explicitly allows that Pell may be truthful, so a rule about lying jurors doesn’t reach this case.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Pell should be removed from the jury, even if he found nothing about the case.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pell searched online for the defendant’s name; the public must be able to see that verdicts rest only on courtroom evidence.

breakdown.analysis: Why remove an honest juror who learned nothing? Because of how it looks. The judge cares about appearances: the public must be able to see that the verdict is clean. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. We need a rule like: if a juror’s conduct makes the public doubt the verdict is based only on the evidence, remove the juror, even if no harm was done.

choices.note: This is the opposite. Under it, Pell stays unless he actually found something, and the judge says to remove him even if he found nothing.

CORRECT. Searching for the defendant gives the public reason to doubt the verdict rests only on the evidence, and the “even if the conduct had no actual effect” clause covers the “even if he’s telling the truth” part. It leads straight to removal.
Points the wrong way. If anything, it suggests Pell, who confessed, should be treated gently, not removed.

Tempting, because lying jurors should go. But the judge says Pell should be removed “even if Pell is telling the truth.” A rule about liars doesn’t apply to an honest juror, so it can’t justify this conclusion.
So? A ranking of fairness against accuracy doesn’t tell the judge to do anything about Pell. It never says to remove a juror.

questions.stimulus: Every adult in the village of Corvale took part in a survey about sleep, and every one of them answered all of its questions. More than 70 percent of the respondents said that they sleep more each night than most other adults in Corvale do.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Most adults in Corvale are mistaken about how much they sleep compared with other adults in Corvale.
Adults in Corvale sleep more each night, on average, than adults in most other villages.
Most adults in Corvale believe that they get enough sleep each night.
At least some of the respondents were wrong about how their sleep compares with that of other Corvale adults.
Adults in Corvale tend to underestimate how much sleep the other adults in their village get each night.
questions.explanation: To sleep more than most other adults in Corvale, a person must be in roughly the top half, and no more than about half of a group can be; since more than 70 percent claimed it, at least some of them answered inaccurately (D). (A) is the trap: the numbers show only that about a fifth or more must be wrong, not most.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Every adult in Corvale answered the survey; 2. More than 70 percent said they sleep more than most other adults in Corvale.

breakdown.analysis: How many people can sleep more than most of their neighbors? Only about half of them. At most roughly the top half can beat a majority of the others. But over 70 percent claimed it. So at least 20 percent or so got it wrong. That’s all the numbers prove. “Some” isn’t “most”: maybe 72 percent claimed it and 50 percent were right, so only 22 percent are mistaken. Because everyone was surveyed, sampling isn’t an escape hatch.

choices.note: Tempting, because clearly people are kidding themselves. But the math only forces about 20 percent to be wrong. Most could be right: the top half answered yes correctly, and the bottom half mostly answered no. Too strong.
Other villages are a different group. The survey compares Corvale adults only with one another.
The survey was about how much people sleep compared with others, not whether they feel they get enough. Unsupported.
CORRECT. No more than about half the adults can sleep more than most of the others, yet over 70 percent said they do. So some answers must be wrong. Modest, and it’s forced by the numbers.
Merely possible. The errors could come from overestimating their own sleep instead. We know some answers are off; we don’t know why.

questions.stimulus: Linguist: One proposed definition holds that a translation is any text that expresses, in one language, the meaning of a text written in another. But consider a three-page English summary of a long German novel. The summary expresses, in English, the meaning of the novel, yet no one would call it a translation of the novel. So the proposed definition cannot be correct as it stands.
questions.stem: The linguist’s argument proceeds by
choices: describing a case that satisfies a proposed definition but that would not ordinarily be counted as an instance of the term being defined
describing a case that would ordinarily be counted as an instance of a term but that a proposed definition of the term fails to include
arguing that because a proposed definition has a counterexample, the term in question cannot be defined at all
rejecting a proposed definition on the grounds that those who proposed it lack expertise in translation
proposing an alternative definition and showing that it fits ordinary usage better than the original definition does
questions.explanation: The summary fits the definition (it expresses the novel’s meaning in another language) but isn’t ordinarily called a translation, so the linguist shows the definition is too broad, which is (A). (B) is the reverse, too narrow: a real translation the definition leaves out; and (C) overstates the conclusion, which says only that this definition is incorrect “as it stands.”

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The proposed definition of “translation” cannot be correct as it stands.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: An English summary of a German novel fits the definition but nobody would call it a translation.

breakdown.analysis: Does the summary fit the definition? Yes: it puts the novel’s meaning into English. Is it a translation? No. So the definition lets in something it shouldn’t. That’s a “too broad” counterexample. Compare: defining a chair as “something you can sit on” lets in a rock. Too narrow would be the reverse: a real chair the definition leaves out. We need the “fits the definition but isn’t the thing” answer.

choices.note: CORRECT. The summary satisfies the definition but isn’t ordinarily counted as a translation. That’s exactly what the linguist does.

Tempting, because it’s also a counterexample method. But it’s the reverse: a genuine translation that the definition excludes, meaning the definition is too narrow. The linguist’s summary is included by the definition and isn’t a real translation.
choices.example: Example of this method: Defining a bird as a flying animal with feathers leaves out the penguin, which is plainly a bird.

choices.note: Too strong. The linguist says only that the definition can’t be correct “as it stands.” Nothing suggests translation can’t be defined at all.
choices.example: Example of this method: Every definition of “game” anyone has offered has a counterexample, so the word cannot be defined.

choices.note: The linguist never mentions who proposed the definition. Wrong method.
choices.example: Example of this method: That definition of poetry came from an engineer, so we can ignore it.

choices.note: The linguist offers no new definition. The argument only knocks down the existing one.
choices.example: Example of this method: Rather than “text in another language,” define translation as “a text meant to stand in for the original,” which fits how we use the word.

questions.stimulus: Glaciologist: Average temperatures in the region around the Brenn Glacier rose during the past decade. Yet over that same decade, the Brenn Glacier advanced. It follows that the Brenn Glacier received more snowfall during the past decade than during the decade before.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the glaciologist’s argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: If a glacier receives more snowfall during a decade than during the decade before, it will advance during that decade even if average temperatures in its region rise.
Most glaciers in regions where average temperatures rose during the past decade retreated during that decade.
Any glacier that has not received more snowfall during a decade than during the decade before does not advance during that decade if average temperatures in its region rise.
Whether a glacier advances or retreats depends more on the snowfall it receives than on average temperatures in its region.
The Brenn Glacier would have advanced even farther during the past decade if average temperatures in its region had not risen.
questions.explanation: (C) says: temperatures rise AND no increase in snowfall → no advance; its contrapositive is temperatures rise AND advance → increased snowfall, and the Brenn facts then yield the conclusion. (A) is the trap: it gives increased snowfall as sufficient for advance, which runs the needed link backwards and leaves open that the Brenn advanced for some other reason with no extra snow.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Brenn Glacier received more snowfall in the past decade than in the decade before.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Regional temperatures rose over the past decade; the Brenn Glacier advanced over the same decade.

breakdown.analysis: Why must the snow have increased? Only if warming plus advance requires more snow. We need: warm AND advance → more snow. In other words, more snow is a necessary condition for a glacier to advance while warming. Contrapositive: warm AND NOT more snow → no advance. The trap gives the sufficient version, more snow → advance, which gets the arrow backwards. Watch the awkward phrasing: the right answer is written in contrapositive form.

choices.note: Tempting, because it ties snowfall, warming, and advance together. But it says more snow → advance. We need advance → more snow. With A, the Brenn could have advanced for some other reason, such as a change in the bedrock or ice flow, with no extra snow at all. This reverses the needed link.
“Most” can’t guarantee anything about the Brenn, and it says nothing about snowfall. Even if most warming-region glaciers retreated, the Brenn could have advanced without extra snow.

CORRECT. In arrows: temperatures rise AND no more snow → no advance. Contrapositive: temperatures rise AND advance → more snow. The Brenn’s region warmed and the glacier advanced, so it got more snow. The conclusion follows.
“Depends more on” is a vague ranking. It doesn’t guarantee that an advance in a warm decade means more snow. The glacier could have advanced for another reason.
Irrelevant. A claim about what would have happened without warming doesn’t tell us anything about the snowfall. It actually assumes the advance, then speculates.

questions.stimulus: Every beekeeper in the Alder Valley cooperative sells honey at the Saturday market. Some of the cooperative’s beekeepers also make candles from their own beeswax. Hence, some people who make candles from their own beeswax sell honey at the Saturday market.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Every guide at the Corran Museum has a degree in art history. Some people with degrees in art history teach at the university. Hence, some guides at the Corran Museum teach at the university.
Most of the employees of the Fennick Bakery work early-morning shifts. Some of the bakery’s employees are students. Hence, some students work early-morning shifts at the Fennick Bakery.
Every glacier guide in Tarvik is certified in first aid. Some people certified in first aid work as lifeguards. Hence, some lifeguards are glacier guides in Tarvik.

All of the moths in the Ilse collection were caught in Brazil, and all of the moths caught in Brazil for that collection were caught before 1950. Hence, all of the moths in the Ilse collection were caught before 1950.

Every member of the Kessel County jury pool has lived in the county for at least a year. Some members of the jury pool are retired. Hence, some retired people have lived in Kessel County for at least a year.
questions.explanation: The argument reasons: all A are B; some A are C; so some C are B. (E) matches exactly: all jury-pool members are year-long residents, some pool members are retired, so some retirees are year-long residents. (D) is also valid, which makes it tempting, but its all-all-all chain is a different pattern; (A) and (C) link the groups through the wrong term and are invalid, and (B) uses “most” plus “some,” which doesn’t guarantee an overlap.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Some people who make candles from their own beeswax sell honey at the Saturday market.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All cooperative beekeepers sell honey at the market; some cooperative beekeepers make candles.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are B; some A are C; so some C are B.

breakdown.analysis: Does it work? Yes. Take the candle-making beekeepers: they’re in the cooperative, and everyone in the cooperative sells honey, so those candle makers sell honey. The shared group (A, the cooperative) is in both premises, and the “all” premise covers it. Map each choice to letters. The match needs all A are B, some A are C, so some C are B. Being valid isn’t enough; the shape has to match.

choices.note: All A (guides) are B (art history degrees); some B teach. The “some” is about art-history graduates, not guides, so the teachers could all be non-guides. Invalid, and a different shape.
Most A work early shifts; some A are students. The students could all be in the minority who don’t work early. “Most” plus “some” doesn’t force an overlap. Invalid.
All A (guides) are B (first-aid certified); some B are lifeguards; so some lifeguards are A. The lifeguards could all be non-guides with first-aid training. Invalid.
Tempting, because it’s valid too. But its shape is all A are B, all B are C, so all A are C: a chain of “alls,” not “all” plus “some.” Valid isn’t the same as parallel.
CORRECT. All A (pool members) are B (year-long residents); some A are C (retired); so some C are B. Same terms in the same places, and valid for the same reason.

questions.stimulus: Entomologist: Some naturalists claim that the decline of the meadow skipper butterfly in the Harrow Hills is due to pesticides sprayed on nearby farms. But their only evidence is that the decline began shortly after the farms started spraying, and that sequence of events by itself hardly shows that the spraying caused the decline. So pesticides are not responsible for the meadow skipper’s decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the entomologist’s reasoning?
choices: It dismisses the naturalists’ claim on the grounds that the naturalists may have a bias against farmers.
It takes the fact that the naturalists’ evidence fails to establish their claim as showing that the claim is false.
It infers that one event caused another from the mere fact that the first event preceded the second.
It presumes, without providing justification, that the meadow skipper population has in fact declined.
It fails to consider that the meadow skipper’s decline may have resulted from more than one cause.
questions.explanation: The entomologist correctly points out that timing alone doesn’t prove the pesticides caused the decline, but then concludes that the pesticides are not responsible, treating a weak argument for a claim as proof the claim is false (B). (C) describes the naturalists’ mistake, which the entomologist identifies rather than commits.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Pesticides are not responsible for the meadow skipper’s decline.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The naturalists’ only evidence is that the decline began after spraying began, and timing alone doesn’t show causation.

breakdown.analysis: Good point about the naturalists: timing alone doesn’t prove cause. But so what? A bad argument for a claim doesn’t make the claim false. The pesticides might still be the culprit; we just don’t know yet. The right conclusion is “unproven,” not “false.” It’s like saying: your only reason for thinking it will rain is that your knee aches, so it won’t rain. We need an answer that says the author treats a failed proof as a disproof.

choices.note: The entomologist never mentions the naturalists’ motives. Wrong flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The naturalists just dislike farmers, so their claim about pesticides can be ignored.

choices.note: CORRECT. The entomologist shows only that the naturalists haven’t proven their case, then concludes the opposite of their claim. Lack of proof isn’t proof of the opposite.
Tempting, because this flaw is in the passage. But it’s the naturalists’ flaw, and the entomologist is the one pointing it out. Watch whose reasoning the question asks about.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The decline began right after spraying started, so the spraying caused it.

choices.note: The entomologist accepts that the decline happened; that isn’t in dispute and isn’t a flaw. Everyone in the passage agrees on it.
Interesting thought, but not the problem. Even if the decline had a single cause, the entomologist would still have no grounds for ruling out pesticides.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The fire was caused by faulty wiring, so the dry weather played no part.

questions.stimulus: Public health officer: In May, Marlow County began a campaign urging residents to wash fresh produce before eating it. From June through September, the county recorded 30 percent fewer cases of foodborne illness than it had during the same months the year before. So the campaign was effective in reducing foodborne illness.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the public health officer’s argument?
choices: Surveys show that most residents who saw the campaign’s advertisements already washed their produce before the campaign began.
Foodborne illness is generally much more common during the summer months than it is during the winter months.
In May, the county also began inspecting restaurants twice as often as it had before.
Neighboring counties with similar food supplies but no such campaign saw no drop in June–September cases from the year before.
Many cases of foodborne illness are never reported to county health officials, especially when symptoms are mild.
questions.explanation: (D) rules out a regional cause, such as a cleaner food supply that year, by showing that similar counties without the campaign saw no drop. (B) is tempting but irrelevant because the comparison already uses the same months in both years; (C) and (A) weaken the argument by offering another cause and suggesting behavior didn’t change; and (E) doesn’t show reporting differed between the two years.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The produce-washing campaign reduced foodborne illness in Marlow County.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After the campaign began in May, June–September cases fell 30 percent from the same months a year earlier.

breakdown.analysis: What if foodborne illness dropped everywhere that summer: a cooler season, or no big outbreak from a contaminated crop? Then the campaign might have done nothing. A drop after a campaign doesn’t show the campaign caused it. We need an answer that rules out a region-wide cause, ideally a comparison group that didn’t get the campaign and didn’t improve.

choices.note: This weakens. If most people already washed their produce, the campaign changed little behavior, so something else probably caused the drop.
Tempting, because it sounds like an explanation for seasonal numbers. But the officer compared June–September with June–September, so the season is already held constant. Irrelevant.
This weakens. Tougher restaurant inspections starting the same month are an alternative cause of the drop.
CORRECT. Similar counties, similar food, no campaign: no drop. So whatever caused Marlow’s drop wasn’t something region-wide, like a cleaner harvest. That makes the campaign a better candidate.
Merely possible problem, and it cuts no particular way. Underreporting happened both years; nothing says it changed. You can’t pick an answer on a possibility.

passages.title: Probate inventories and household goods
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Passage A

For most of the eighteenth century, the households of the Brennick district left almost no written trace of their daily lives. Few kept diaries, and fewer still kept accounts. Yet when a householder died leaving property to be divided, local law required two neighbors to walk through the house and list every movable object in it, room by room, with a value beside each. Some eleven thousand of these probate inventories survive for the years 1690 to 1780, and in her study of them the historian Renata Kolbe found what she calls “a quiet revolution in the kitchen.”

In inventories from the 1690s, earthenware plates appear in fewer than one household in ten; by the 1760s they appear in more than half. Mirrors, clocks, and printed books follow the same rising curve. What makes the pattern striking is that it is not confined to the prosperous. Among households whose total estate fell in the lowest third, the share owning earthenware rose almost as quickly as among the wealthiest.

Kolbe argues that this cannot be explained by rising pay, since the district’s wage records show day rates nearly flat across the period. Instead, she proposes that ordinary families changed how they worked: wives and children took in spinning and other piecework, and the added income was spent on goods that could be bought rather than made. The inventories, on this view, record not merely what people owned but a deliberate choice to labor more in order to consume more.

Whatever one makes of that interpretation, the inventories themselves offer something no other source can: a census of objects, compiled by eyewitnesses, across thousands of ordinary homes.

Passage B

Historians who wish to recover the material lives of ordinary people have understandably seized on probate inventories, which appear to offer exactly what diaries and account books do not. But the impression of completeness these documents give is misleading, and conclusions about changing consumption drawn from them require more caution than they usually receive.

To begin with, inventories were not taken for everyone. They were drawn up when an estate had to be divided or debts settled, and the very poorest, whose possessions hardly justified the trouble of appraisal, were seldom inventoried at all. A household in the lowest third of a body of inventories is thus in the lowest third of those who owned enough to be counted—a group considerably better off than the population at large.

The people inventoried, moreover, were disproportionately old. A typical decedent had spent decades accumulating goods, so an inventory records a lifetime’s acquisitions rather than the habits of any one moment. An apparent rise in ownership across several decades may partly reflect changes in who lived long enough to leave an inventory, and at what age.

Finally, appraisers listed what they judged worth listing. Cheap items were often lumped together as “sundries,” and the threshold for a separate line varied from one appraiser to the next and drifted over time. The first appearance of an object in the inventories may therefore record a change in appraisers’ habits as much as a change in households’ possessions. None of this makes inventories worthless; read alongside other records, they remain indispensable. Read alone, they are an uncertain census.
