passages.title: Liquidated damages and the penalty doctrine
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
When the parties to a contract foresee that a breach would cause losses that are hard to measure, they often agree in advance on the sum the breaching party will pay. Courts in common-law jurisdictions have long enforced such liquidated damages clauses, but only within limits. A clause that represents a reasonable estimate of the harm a breach would cause is upheld; one that sets a sum far exceeding any plausible loss, so that its evident purpose is to frighten a party into performing, is struck down as a penalty, and the injured party is left to prove its actual damages in the ordinary way.

The legal scholar Anselm Rudd has argued that this penalty doctrine is a relic. Courts enforce a contract, he notes, because its terms reflect what the parties judged to be in their interest, and a party that agrees to pay a large fixed sum for breach presumably receives something in exchange: a higher price, a faster schedule, or the contract itself, which the other side might not have signed without the assurance. Striking down the clause after the fact deprives the injured party of what it bargained for and hands the breaching party a benefit it never paid for. Rudd would therefore enforce any damages clause agreed to by commercial parties of comparable sophistication, however large the sum.

Rudd’s argument has real force where it is strongest: between well-advised firms, a court that second-guesses a negotiated figure may simply be substituting its own judgment of risk for theirs. Yet the argument does not clarify how a court is to know that a clause was in fact bargained over. Large firms routinely contract on standard forms that neither side reads closely, and a damages clause buried in such a form may reflect no one’s considered judgment at all. Rudd’s test of comparable sophistication describes the parties, not the transaction; it cannot distinguish a figure both sides weighed from one that one side’s lawyers inserted and the other side’s never noticed.

Rudd also assumes that the only parties affected by an enforced penalty are the two who signed. But a firm that must pay a sum many times its counterparty’s actual loss may be unable to pay its other creditors, its employees, or its own suppliers, none of whom agreed to anything. When a maker of hospital equipment owes a crushing sum for a two-week delay, the cost falls partly on those who depend on its continued operation.

None of this rescues the doctrine’s traditional rationale, which treated penalties as objectionable simply because they coerce performance; Rudd is right that a promise backed by a strong incentive is not, for that reason, unfair. What the doctrine may protect instead is the integrity of bargaining and the interests of outsiders to the contract—purposes that suggest a narrower rule than the one courts now apply, but not its abolition.

passages.title: Bitter nectar in the Varrow lily
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
Nectar is usually understood as a payment: a plant offers sugar so that animals will carry its pollen from flower to flower. It is therefore puzzling that the nectar of the Varrow lily, a perennial of high meadows pollinated chiefly by bumblebees, contains a bitter alkaloid that bees, when offered a choice in laboratory trials, plainly avoid. Why would a plant make its reward less rewarding?

The usual answer has been that the alkaloid deters nectar thieves, insects that drink nectar without transferring pollen. But the botanist Leni Carrow points out that the likeliest thieves, ants, are scarce in the meadows where the lily grows, and that the few ants present seldom climb its stalks. Whatever the alkaloid does, she argues, it must do to the bees themselves.

Carrow’s proposal is that the bitterness shortens visits. A Varrow lily bears many flowers on a single stalk, and a bee that finds sweet nectar tends to work its way through flower after flower on the same plant. Each such move does little for the lily: it carries pollen from one of the plant’s flowers to another, and the seeds that result are inbred and frequently fail. A bee that tastes the alkaloid, by contrast, takes a sip or two and leaves, and because it is still hungry, it flies on to another plant. Suppose a bee arrives carrying pollen from a distant lily. If it visits eight flowers, most of the pollen it leaves on the later ones will be the plant’s own, picked up from the earlier ones; if it visits only two, nearly all the pollen it leaves will be foreign.

To test the idea, Carrow’s team drained the nectar from flowers in a meadow population and refilled them with a sugar solution that either contained the alkaloid at its natural concentration or lacked it. Bees on alkaloid-free plants visited an average of 6.1 flowers per plant; bees on alkaloid plants visited 2.4. When the team later used genetic markers to identify the fathers of the resulting seeds, 71 percent of the seeds from alkaloid plants proved to have been sired by other plants, against 38 percent of the seeds from alkaloid-free plants.

These results make Carrow’s account considerably more persuasive than the thief-deterrence view, at least for this species. Yet the experiment was conducted in a dense stand, where a departing bee rarely had to fly more than a few meters to reach another lily. Where the plants grow sparsely, a bee repelled by bitter nectar might as readily turn to some other kind of flower altogether, carrying the lily’s pollen to no purpose. Whether the alkaloid pays for itself across the lily’s whole range thus remains an open question.

passages.title: Oriel Fane’s stage directions
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
The plays of Oriel Fane, written in the 1920s and 1930s, are notorious for their stage directions. A single direction in The Glass Orchard runs to nearly two pages, describing not only the set but the smell of the room, the history of its furniture, and what one character “has never told anyone and never will.” In an influential study, the critic Tomas Hallard argues that such passages were never meant to guide a production. Fane, on this view, was a novelist at heart who wrote for the reader in an armchair; the directions are prose fiction lodged inside a script, and directors who try to stage them misunderstand the kind of text they are handling.

Hallard’s reading has the merit of taking the directions seriously as writing, which earlier critics, who dismissed them as self-indulgent padding, did not do. But it fails to clarify what it would mean for a direction to be written “for the reader” rather than for the stage. Much of what Fane specifies is plainly theatrical: the exact moment a lamp is to dim, the number of paces between two chairs. Hallard treats the unstageable details as the essence of the directions and the stageable ones as residue, but he offers no reason for weighting them this way.

The reading also relies on an assumption Hallard never defends: that a direction can serve a production only by specifying something an audience will see or hear. Only on that assumption does the presence of unstageable material show that Fane was writing for readers. Hallard cites in support the fact that the directions in the printed editions are far longer than those in the promptbooks surviving from the premieres, productions in which Fane was closely involved. But that evidence cuts both ways. It is consistent with Fane’s having expanded the directions for readers, and equally consistent with her having set down in print what she had conveyed to performers by other means.

The second possibility gains support from a fact Hallard’s account cannot easily absorb. Actors who worked with Fane recalled that she read the full directions aloud at the first rehearsal of each play and never referred to them again. On this evidence, the detail about what a character has never told anyone was not meant to be shown; it was meant to be known by the actor, and to shape everything she did onstage. If so, the directions are neither instructions in the ordinary sense nor fiction for readers, but something closer to a private briefing made public, and the directors Hallard faults may have understood Fane better than he does.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately characterizes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A criticizes a historian’s use of a particular kind of record, and passage B defends that use against the criticism.
Passage A describes a body of evidence and a conclusion drawn from it, and passage B argues that the same evidence supports the opposite conclusion.
Both passages draw conclusions from probate inventories, but the conclusions in passage B concern a different region and period.
Passage A presents conclusions a historian has drawn from a particular kind of record, and passage B raises general concerns about that kind of record that bear on such conclusions.
Passage A argues that a particular kind of record is the only reliable source on its subject, and passage B argues that the record is entirely unreliable.
questions.explanation: Passage A reports Kolbe’s findings and interpretation from the Brennick inventories; passage B, without mentioning Kolbe, raises general cautions about inventories (who was counted, the age of decedents, appraisers’ habits) that apply to findings like hers. That is D. A reverses the roles. B fails because passage B never argues that ownership fell or that the opposite conclusion holds; it says such conclusions need more caution. E is too extreme on both sides: passage B says inventories ‘remain indispensable.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how passage B relates to passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The opening of each passage and the last two sentences of passage B.

breakdown.analysis: Label each passage first. A: here’s what Kolbe found in the inventories and how she explains it. B: inventories look complete but aren’t, so be careful with conclusions drawn from them. B never names Kolbe, but its worries hit her findings squarely (it even uses her “lowest third”). So we want: A presents conclusions from a type of record; B raises general cautions about that type of record. Watch the strength of B: it’s cautious, not hostile. It ends by calling inventories “indispensable.”

choices.note: Reversed. A doesn’t criticize Kolbe; it reports her work and praises the inventories. B is the one with reservations, and it doesn’t defend anything.

Tempting, because B does suggest the rise in ownership “may partly reflect” other things. But “partly” and “may” are not “the opposite conclusion.” B never says ownership didn’t rise. It says the evidence is less certain than it looks.
B draws no conclusions about any region or period. It talks about inventories in general.
CORRECT. A: Kolbe’s conclusions from probate inventories. B: general concerns about probate inventories (who’s counted, age, appraisers’ habits) that bear directly on conclusions like hers.
Too strong, twice. A says inventories offer something no other source can, which isn’t “the only reliable source.” B explicitly says they are not worthless and remain indispensable.

questions.stem: By characterizing probate inventories read alone as “an uncertain census” (last sentence of passage B), the author of passage B most likely means that such inventories
choices: record only a small fraction of the objects that households of the period actually owned
appear to provide a comprehensive count of household possessions but cannot by themselves be relied on to do so
were compiled by appraisers who were often unsure of the monetary value of the objects they listed
survive in numbers too small to support generalizations about the population as a whole
provide accurate information about wealthy households but unreliable information about poor ones
questions.explanation: Passage B opens by saying ‘the impression of completeness these documents give is misleading’ and closes by saying inventories read alone are ‘an uncertain census.’ A census is a complete count, so the phrase means the inventories look like a full count but cannot be trusted as one without other records: B. A is too strong; passage B never estimates how much went unrecorded. C twists ‘uncertain’ into appraisers’ uncertainty about values, which the passage never mentions. E is tempting because of the second paragraph, but the age and appraiser problems apply to every household, and B never calls wealthy households’ inventories accurate.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Figure out what “an uncertain census” means in context.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first paragraph of passage B (“impression of completeness…is misleading”) and its last two sentences. Note that passage A ends by calling inventories “a census of objects.”

breakdown.analysis: A census is a full count. B’s whole point is that inventories look like a full count and aren’t quite one: some people aren’t counted, the counted skew old, and cheap stuff gets lumped. “Read alone” matters too: alongside other records they’re indispensable. So prephrase: they seem like a complete count but you can’t trust them as one by themselves. Bonus: B is quietly answering A’s last line.

choices.note: Too strong. B says some cheap items were lumped and some households were skipped. It never says most objects went unrecorded.
CORRECT. “Census” = the look of a complete count; “uncertain” = can’t be relied on as one; “read alone” = by themselves. All three pieces match.
Tempting if you grab the word “uncertain.” But B’s worry is about what got listed, not whether appraisers knew the prices. Values never come up as a problem.
B never says there are too few inventories. Passage A mentions eleven thousand. B’s worry is who is in the sample, not how big it is.
Half-right at best. Paragraph two is about the poorest being left out, but B’s age and appraiser problems apply to everyone. B never says rich households’ inventories are accurate.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a criticism that the author of passage B would be most likely to make regarding Kolbe’s finding about households whose total estate fell in the lowest third?
choices: Those households were probably considerably more prosperous than the poorest households in the district.
The value of the earthenware in those households was probably overstated by the appraisers.
Those households probably acquired most of their earthenware through inheritance rather than purchase.
The inventories of those households were probably less complete than the inventories of the wealthiest households.
Earthenware probably became common among those households only after it had become common among the wealthiest.
questions.explanation: Passage B’s second paragraph says the poorest were seldom inventoried, so a household in the lowest third of a body of inventories belongs to ‘a group considerably better off than the population at large.’ Applied to Kolbe, that is A: her ‘lowest third’ aren’t the district’s poor. D is the main trap: B does say cheap items were lumped as ‘sundries,’ but it never claims poorer households’ inventories were less complete than richer ones’. B, C and E introduce claims passage B never makes; E even contradicts the data in passage A.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the objection B’s author would raise against Kolbe’s “lowest third” finding.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A’s second paragraph (the lowest-third finding) and passage B’s second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: So what if poor-ish inventories show earthenware? Who were these “poor” households? B practically answers by name: the lowest third of inventories is the lowest third of people who owned enough to be counted. The really poor aren’t in the data at all. So Kolbe’s claim that the change reached beyond the prosperous rests on a group that was better off than it looks. Prephrase: those households weren’t really the poor.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is B’s second paragraph aimed straight at Kolbe: the lowest third of inventoried estates is still “considerably better off than the population at large.”
B never questions the values appraisers assigned. Its complaint about appraisers is what they bothered to list, not how they priced it.
Inheritance never comes up. B’s age point is about a lifetime of buying, not about goods passed down.
Tempting, because B does say cheap items were lumped as “sundries.” But B never ties that to poorer households or compares rich and poor inventories. You’d have to supply that link yourself.
Not B’s claim, and it contradicts A’s data that the poor-end share rose “almost as quickly” as the rich-end share. B never discusses timing between groups.

questions.stem: The authors of both passages would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: The rise in ownership of earthenware recorded in the inventories reflects a change in how ordinary families worked.
The poorest households of the period were seldom inventoried because their possessions were not worth appraising.
Probate inventories from the eighteenth century are more reliable than those from earlier periods.
Probate inventories provide a complete record of the objects found in the households they describe.
Probate inventories provide information about the possessions of ordinary households that is difficult to obtain from other kinds of records.
questions.explanation: Passage A says inventories offer ‘something no other source can,’ noting that few households kept diaries or accounts; passage B says inventories appear to offer ‘exactly what diaries and account books do not’ and ‘remain indispensable.’ Both therefore accept E. A is the strongest trap: it is Kolbe’s interpretation, but passage A’s author pointedly withholds endorsement (‘Whatever one makes of that interpretation’), and passage B never addresses it. B is stated only in passage B, C in neither, and D is denied by passage B.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim both authors would accept.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A’s first and last paragraphs; passage B’s first sentence and last three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: For agreement, both authors need to be on record. Start with what B concedes, since B is the skeptic. B concedes inventories seem to offer what diaries and accounts don’t, and that they’re indispensable. A says they offer what no other source can. That overlap is the answer. Watch out for Kolbe’s theory: the author of A reports it but doesn’t sign on to it.

choices.note: Tempting, because it’s the big idea in passage A. But it’s Kolbe’s view. A’s author says “Whatever one makes of that interpretation,” which is a deliberate refusal to commit. And B never touches it. Know the difference between an author and the scholar the author describes.
Only B says this. A never talks about who was left out of the inventories.
Neither passage compares periods for reliability. Out of scope.
A’s author might lean this way (“every movable object,” “a census”), but B flatly denies it: the completeness is “misleading.” That’s a disagreement, not an agreement.

CORRECT. A: “something no other source can.” B: they offer what diaries and account books do not and “remain indispensable.” Both say inventories give you something about ordinary homes that is hard to get elsewhere.

questions.stem: In passage A, the reference to the district’s wage records (third paragraph) serves primarily to
choices: provide evidence that households in the lowest third were poorer than their inventories suggest
illustrate the kinds of written records that ordinary households in the district kept
support Kolbe’s rejection of one possible explanation of the pattern found in the inventories
show that the prices of earthenware and similar goods fell during the period
suggest that the inventories understate the total income of ordinary families
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the rise in ownership ‘cannot be explained by rising pay, since the district’s wage records show day rates nearly flat.’ The wage records are Kolbe’s reason for ruling out the obvious explanation before offering her own, which is C. B fails because passage A says few households kept accounts; wage records are district records, not household ones. D is never stated, and A and E misdescribe what the records are used to show.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the wage records are mentioned.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of passage A’s third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence with the word “since” in it: rising pay can’t explain the change, since wages were flat. Wage records are the evidence for ruling out an alternative. Then Kolbe offers her own explanation (more family labor). Prephrase: to knock out the “people just earned more” explanation.

choices.note: The wage records say nothing about the lowest-third inventories. They show day rates were flat, nothing more.
Opposite of the passage. A says few households kept accounts. Wage records belong to the district, and they aren’t mentioned as an example of household record-keeping.
CORRECT. Flat wages rule out “rising pay” as the cause, clearing the way for Kolbe’s piecework explanation.
Prices never come up. The records are about wages, not the cost of plates.

Interesting thought, since Kolbe says families earned extra from piecework. But the wage records aren’t used to say anything about the inventories understating income. Inventories don’t record income at all.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true of the Brennick inventories, would most weaken the bearing on Kolbe’s findings of the concern raised in the third paragraph of passage B?
choices: In each decade, ownership of earthenware rose about as quickly among householders who died young as among those who died old, and the average age at death of inventoried householders changed little over the period.
Appraisers in the 1760s were more likely than appraisers in the 1690s to list inexpensive objects individually rather than as sundries.
The number of inventories surviving from the 1760s is considerably larger than the number surviving from the 1690s.
Many of the households in the lowest third of the inventories owned no land.
Most of the householders who were inventoried had lived in the district for their entire adult lives.
questions.explanation: Passage B’s third paragraph warns that inventoried people were disproportionately old, so inventories show lifetime accumulation, and that an apparent rise may reflect changes in who lived long enough to leave an inventory, and at what age. A answers both halves: the age mix was stable, and the rise shows up among the young dead too. B is the main trap, but it concerns the fourth paragraph’s appraiser problem, and it would strengthen that concern rather than weaken anything. C is irrelevant to proportions, D bears on the second paragraph, and E has nothing to do with age.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that defuses B’s age worry as applied to Kolbe.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B’s third paragraph (age of decedents), and Kolbe’s rising curve in passage A’s second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: First pin down which concern. Paragraph three of B is the age one: 1. inventories record a lifetime of buying, not current habits; 2. the rise could come from a change in who died, and how old they were. To defuse it, we want evidence that age isn’t driving Kolbe’s curve: the age mix held steady, and the rise appears among younger decedents too. It’s like a claim that “people read more now” based on obituaries: show that the age of the dead didn’t change and young readers rose too, and the age objection is gone.

choices.note: CORRECT. Stable age at death kills the “changes in who lived long enough” explanation, and a rise among the young dead shows the change isn’t just a lifetime of slow accumulation. Both halves of the third-paragraph concern are handled.

Tempting, because it’s about the inventories over time. But it’s the fourth paragraph’s appraiser concern, not the third’s. And it makes that concern worse: if later appraisers listed cheap things more often, some of Kolbe’s rise could be an artifact of listing habits.
Irrelevant. Kolbe’s figures are shares (one in ten, more than half), so the raw number of surviving inventories doesn’t touch the age problem.
Wrong paragraph. Who counts as poor is B’s second-paragraph concern. And landlessness says nothing about age.
Living in the district your whole life isn’t the same as dying young or old. Doesn’t touch the age mix.

questions.stem: The author of passage B suggests that historians who draw conclusions about changing consumption from probate inventories have often been too
choices: pessimistic
dismissive
specialized
incautious
hesitant
questions.explanation: Passage B’s first paragraph says such conclusions ‘require more caution than they usually receive,’ and it describes historians as having ‘seized on’ inventories. So these historians have been too incautious: D. B (dismissive) and E (hesitant) point the wrong way; the complaint is that historians trust the sources too readily, not that they reject or hold back from them.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the one word for B’s complaint about these historians.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B’s first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: B says the conclusions “require more caution than they usually receive.” Not enough caution = incautious. Before you look, decide the direction: B thinks historians trust inventories too much, not too little.

choices.note: Wrong direction. Pessimists would doubt the inventories. B thinks historians have been too trusting.
Also wrong direction. Historians “seized on” inventories; they didn’t dismiss them.
B never says historians are too narrow in focus. Off topic.
CORRECT. “More caution than they usually receive” is exactly “too incautious.”
Opposite. Hesitant historians would be the cautious ones B wants more of.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The penalty doctrine should be abolished because it permits courts to substitute their own judgment of risk for the judgment of commercial parties.
The traditional rationale for the penalty doctrine remains sound, although courts have applied the doctrine to more clauses than that rationale can justify.
Although Rudd’s case against the penalty doctrine has some force, it overlooks considerations that may justify keeping a narrower version of the doctrine.
Because damages clauses in commercial contracts are rarely the product of genuine bargaining, courts should scrutinize every such clause closely.
Rudd’s argument shows that the penalty doctrine harms sophisticated commercial parties, but it fails to show that the doctrine harms anyone else.
questions.explanation: The author grants that Rudd’s argument ‘has real force,’ then identifies two things it overlooks (whether a clause was actually bargained over, and harm to outsiders), and concludes that these purposes support ‘a narrower rule than the one courts now apply, but not its abolition.’ That is C. A is Rudd’s position, not the author’s. B is the trap for readers who notice the author wants a narrower rule, but the author explicitly says nothing ‘rescues the doctrine’s traditional rationale.’ D is too strong (‘rarely,’ ‘every’), and E garbles the third and fourth paragraphs.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the author’s overall point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of the third paragraph and the whole last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Find the author’s turn: Rudd’s argument “has real force… Yet” it fails to clarify one thing and assumes another. Then the wrap-up: the old rationale is dead, but the doctrine may protect other things, so narrow it, don’t abolish it. The main point needs both halves: Rudd has a point, but his case misses things that justify keeping a narrower doctrine.

choices.note: Rudd’s view, not the author’s. The author ends by saying the doctrine should be narrowed, “not” abolished. Always ask whose view a main-point answer states.
Tempting, because the author does want a narrower rule. But the author says nothing “rescues the doctrine’s traditional rationale.” The old reason is rejected; the new reasons are different ones.
CORRECT. Grants Rudd’s force, names that he overlooks things (bargaining, outsiders), and lands on narrowing instead of abolishing.
Too strong. The author says standard-form clauses “may” reflect no one’s judgment. Nothing says clauses are rarely bargained over or that every one needs close scrutiny.
Garbled. Rudd argues the doctrine deprives injured parties of their bargain; the author’s outsider point is about harm from enforcing penalties, not harm from the doctrine.

questions.stem: According to the passage, when a court strikes down a damages clause as a penalty, the injured party
choices: receives no compensation for the breach
must prove its actual damages in the ordinary way
receives a sum the court judges to be a reasonable estimate of the harm
may recover the stipulated sum from the breaching party’s creditors
may recover the stipulated sum only if the breach was intentional
questions.explanation: The last sentence of the first paragraph says that when a clause is struck down as a penalty, ‘the injured party is left to prove its actual damages in the ordinary way.’ That is B. A is the trap for a reader who equates striking the clause with denying all recovery. C confuses the test for upholding a clause (a reasonable estimate) with what happens after one is struck. D and E are never stated.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what happens to the injured party when a penalty clause is struck down.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of the first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Pure detail. The first paragraph says it: the clause is struck down, and the injured party “is left to prove its actual damages in the ordinary way.” Find the answer that says that.

choices.note: Too strong. Losing the clause doesn’t mean losing everything. The injured party can still prove its actual damages.
CORRECT. Nearly word for word from the end of the first paragraph.
Mixes up two ideas. “Reasonable estimate” is the test for upholding a clause. Nothing says the court substitutes its own figure.
Creditors come up only in the fourth paragraph, as people who might be hurt by an enforced penalty. Nobody recovers from them.
Intent is never mentioned. Made up.

questions.stem: In saying that Rudd’s test of comparable sophistication “describes the parties, not the transaction” (end of the third paragraph), the author most likely means that the test
choices: looks to the size of the stipulated sum rather than to the loss actually caused by the breach
applies to contracts between firms but not to contracts between a firm and an individual
fails to take into account whether the contracting parties were equally sophisticated
requires a court to examine each party’s reasons for entering into the contract
considers who the contracting parties are but not whether the particular clause was actually negotiated
questions.explanation: The third paragraph’s complaint is that firms of comparable sophistication may still sign standard forms whose damages clauses ‘no one’ considered, so the test ‘cannot distinguish a figure both sides weighed from one that…the other side’s never noticed.’ The test looks at the kind of parties involved, not at how the clause came about: E. B is the trap, reading ‘parties’ as a point about which kinds of parties are covered, which the sentence is not about. C reverses the test, and A and D describe things the test never does.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decode “describes the parties, not the transaction.”

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last three sentences of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence after the semicolon: the test “cannot distinguish a figure both sides weighed from one that one side’s lawyers inserted and the other side’s never noticed.” So the test asks who signed (two sophisticated firms), not what happened in this deal (was the clause actually bargained over?). It’s like judging whether a chess game was well played by checking that both players are grandmasters. Grandmasters still blunder.

choices.note: The size of the sum isn’t the issue here. Rudd’s test ignores size entirely (“however large the sum”).
Tempting, because Rudd’s test does refer to “commercial parties.” But the phrase isn’t about which contracts are covered; it’s about what the test checks within a covered contract.
Reversed. Comparable sophistication is exactly what the test does take into account.
The test examines no one’s reasons. If anything, the author faults it for not looking at how the deal was made.
CORRECT. “Parties” = who signed; “transaction” = whether this clause was actually weighed by both sides. The test checks the first and misses the second.

questions.stem: The author mentions a maker of hospital equipment (fourth paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: illustrate how enforcing a penalty can impose costs on people who did not agree to the contract
show that firms of comparable sophistication frequently contract on standard forms
provide an example of a damages clause that reasonably estimated the harm a breach would cause
suggest that penalty clauses are more common in some industries than in others
demonstrate that a short delay in performance rarely causes a significant loss
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph argues that Rudd overlooks outsiders: a firm owing a huge penalty may be unable to pay creditors, employees, or suppliers, ‘none of whom agreed to anything.’ The hospital-equipment maker makes that concrete, since the cost of its crushing penalty ‘falls partly on those who depend on its continued operation.’ That is A. B belongs to the third paragraph, C misdescribes the clause (it is a crushing sum, not a reasonable estimate), and D and E are never claimed.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the hospital-equipment example is there.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The paragraph’s claim comes first: Rudd assumes only the two signers are affected, but a crushing penalty can hit creditors, workers, suppliers. Then the example: a hospital-equipment maker hit with a huge penalty, and the cost spreads to people who depend on it. Prephrase: a concrete case of outsiders bearing the cost of an enforced penalty.

choices.note: CORRECT. The example shows the cost of an enforced penalty falling on people who never signed anything.
Wrong paragraph. Standard forms are the third paragraph’s concern; this example says nothing about how the contract was drafted.
Opposite. The sum is “crushing” for a two-week delay, which is the picture of a penalty, not a reasonable estimate.
No comparison across industries is made. The hospital setting just makes the outsiders vivid.
Tempting, since a crushing sum for a short delay hints the loss was small. But the example isn’t there to make a general claim about delays; it’s there to show who else pays.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward the traditional rationale for the penalty doctrine can best be described as one of
choices: nostalgia
rejection
ambivalence
endorsement
indifference
questions.explanation: The traditional rationale treated penalties as objectionable ‘simply because they coerce performance.’ The author says ‘None of this rescues’ that rationale and agrees with Rudd that a strongly incentivized promise ‘is not, for that reason, unfair.’ That is rejection: B. D is the trap, because the author does favor keeping a narrower doctrine, but on different grounds, so the support is for the doctrine, not its traditional rationale. C fails because the author shows no mixed feelings on this specific point.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Name the author’s attitude toward the old reason for the penalty doctrine.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of the last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Read the stem closely: it’s about the traditional rationale, not the doctrine. The rationale is “penalties are bad because they coerce performance.” The author: nothing “rescues” it, and Rudd “is right” that a strong incentive isn’t unfair. So the author throws it out. The author wants to keep a narrower doctrine for different reasons. Keep the rule and the reason for it apart.

choices.note: Nostalgia would mean fondness for the old view. The author dismisses it.
CORRECT. “None of this rescues the doctrine’s traditional rationale” plus agreement with Rudd on that point: a clear rejection.
Tempting if you’re summing up the author’s whole view (against abolition, but against the old reasoning). On the rationale itself, there’s no mixed feeling.
The big trap. The author supports keeping the doctrine, but on new grounds (bargaining integrity, outsiders). The traditional rationale is exactly what the author lets go.
The author takes a clear stand on it, so not indifferent.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question the author’s argument in the third paragraph?
choices: Most commercial contracts between large firms are drafted on standard forms supplied by one of the parties.
Courts applying the penalty doctrine frequently misjudge the losses that a breach of contract actually causes.
Firms required to pay large stipulated sums for breach often become unable to pay their other creditors.
Even in contracts otherwise drafted on standard forms, damages clauses are almost always negotiated separately and revised by both sides before signing.
Small businesses that contract with large firms rarely read the standard terms they agree to.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph argues that Rudd cannot tell whether a clause was bargained over, because a damages clause ‘buried in’ a standard form ‘may reflect no one’s considered judgment.’ D says damages clauses, even in standard-form contracts, are almost always separately negotiated and revised by both sides, which removes the scenario the argument depends on. B is the main trap: it supports Rudd’s general case against judicial second-guessing, but it does not touch the third paragraph’s point about whether clauses are actually bargained over. A and E strengthen or sidestep the argument, and C bears on the fourth paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most damages the author’s “was it really bargained over?” argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third paragraph, especially the standard-form sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Lay out the argument: 1. firms contract on standard forms nobody reads closely; 2. so a damages clause in one may reflect no one’s judgment; 3. so Rudd’s sophistication test can’t tell real bargains from unnoticed boilerplate. So what if the form is boilerplate? Maybe the damages clause isn’t. To weaken, show that damages clauses in particular do get bargained over, even in standard-form deals. Careful: helping Rudd in general isn’t the same as hurting this specific argument.

choices.note: Strengthens the author. More standard-form contracts means more room for unnoticed clauses.
Tempting, because it backs Rudd’s point that courts shouldn’t second-guess. But the third paragraph is about whether clauses were actually negotiated, and this answer says nothing about that.
Wrong paragraph. This supports the fourth paragraph’s outsider argument and doesn’t touch the bargaining point.
CORRECT. If damages clauses are separately negotiated and revised by both sides even within standard forms, the worry that such a clause reflects “no one’s considered judgment” mostly disappears.
Rudd’s test covers commercial parties of comparable sophistication, not small businesses dealing with large firms. Out of scope, and if anything it supports the author’s premise.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Courts currently strike down too few damages clauses as penalties.
Courts should never enforce damages clauses that appear in standard-form contracts.
In deciding whether to enforce a large stipulated sum, a court could appropriately consider evidence about how the clause came to be included in the contract.
The penalty doctrine is justified chiefly by the fact that penalty clauses coerce performance.
Rudd’s proposal would be acceptable if it were limited to contracts in which neither party has creditors.
questions.explanation: The author faults Rudd’s test for ignoring whether a clause was ‘in fact bargained over’ and says the doctrine may properly protect ‘the integrity of bargaining.’ That commits the author to the view that how a clause got into the contract is relevant to whether it should be enforced: C. A is the strongest trap, but it reverses the conclusion: the author wants ‘a narrower rule than the one courts now apply,’ which would strike down fewer clauses, not more. B is too strong (standard-form clauses ‘may’ reflect no one’s judgment), D is the rationale the author rejects, and E ignores both the employees and suppliers in the fourth paragraph and the bargaining concern in the third.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim the author’s reasoning commits the author to.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third paragraph and the last sentence of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so test each choice against the author’s words. Two clues: 1. Rudd’s test is faulted for not asking whether a clause “was in fact bargained over”; 2. the doctrine “may protect… the integrity of bargaining.” If those matter, a court should be allowed to look at how the clause got into the deal. Watch the direction word “narrower”: a narrower penalty rule strikes down fewer clauses, not more.

choices.note: The big trap. It sounds like the author is defending the doctrine, so maybe the author wants more clauses struck. But the author calls for “a narrower rule than the one courts now apply.” A narrower rule catches fewer clauses. This reverses the author.
Too strong. Standard-form clauses “may” reflect no one’s judgment. “Never enforce” goes far beyond that.
CORRECT. The author’s complaint about Rudd and the “integrity of bargaining” purpose both make the history of the clause relevant to whether a court should enforce it.
This is the traditional rationale, and the author says nothing “rescues” it.
Half-right at best. Creditors are only one of the outsider groups (employees and suppliers too), and the bargaining problem in the third paragraph would remain anyway.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The alkaloid in the Varrow lily’s nectar is best explained as a defense against insects that drink nectar without carrying pollen between plants.
Carrow’s experiment shows that the bitter nectar of the Varrow lily increases cross-pollination wherever the species grows.
Because bumblebees avoid bitter nectar, lilies that produce it receive fewer pollinator visits and therefore set fewer seeds than other lilies.
Carrow’s view that the lily’s bitter nectar promotes cross-pollination by shortening bee visits is well supported, though its reach is uncertain.
Nectar should be understood not as a payment to pollinators but as a means by which plants control the movements of the animals that visit them.
questions.explanation: The passage poses a puzzle, sets aside the thief-deterrence answer, explains and tests Carrow’s visit-shortening account, and ends by calling it persuasive for dense stands but open across the lily’s range, which is D. B is the most tempting trap, but the last paragraph says the opposite of ‘wherever the species grows’: sparse stands are an open question. A is the view the passage rejects.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the main point: the claim the whole passage is organized to support, including the author’s final verdict.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First and last paragraphs for the frame; the third and fourth paragraphs for Carrow’s account and test.

breakdown.analysis: What does the author actually conclude? Not just ‘Carrow is right’: the last paragraph says her account is ‘considerably more persuasive’ than the rival, ‘at least for this species,’ and then flags sparse stands as an open question. So we need an answer that says: Carrow’s explanation (bitterness → shorter visits → more outcrossing) is well supported, with a reservation about its scope. Main-point answers must match the author’s degree of commitment, not just the topic.

choices.note: Wrong. This is the ‘usual answer’ the second paragraph sets aside, because ants are scarce where the lily grows. Picking it means you stopped reading after the first view.
Tempting, because the experiment does support Carrow. But ‘wherever the species grows’ is exactly what the author refuses to say: the last paragraph leaves sparse stands open. Too strong.

Wrong. The passage never says alkaloid plants set fewer seeds; the point is that more of their seeds are outcrossed. This takes the first paragraph’s puzzle and turns it into a conclusion the passage never draws.

CORRECT. It names Carrow’s mechanism (shorter visits, more cross-pollination), says it’s well supported (the fourth paragraph’s results), and keeps the final reservation about range. That’s the whole passage, at the author’s level of confidence.
Too broad. The passage is about one lily’s nectar, not a new theory of nectar in general. The first sentence’s ‘payment’ idea is background that sets up the puzzle, not a claim the author overturns.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in Carrow’s experiment, bees on plants whose flowers had been refilled with alkaloid-free solution
choices: visited fewer flowers per plant than did bees on plants refilled with the alkaloid
visited more than twice as many flowers per plant as did bees on plants refilled with the alkaloid
left mostly foreign pollen on the flowers they visited after the first two
typically took only a sip or two of nectar before leaving each plant
often left the stand altogether to forage on other kinds of flowers
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph gives 6.1 flowers per plant on alkaloid-free plants against 2.4 on alkaloid plants, and 6.1 is more than twice 2.4, so B. A reverses the comparison, and D describes bees that taste the alkaloid, not bees on alkaloid-free plants.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the bees on the alkaloid-free plants in the experiment.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, the sentence with 6.1 and 2.4.

breakdown.analysis: Pure detail. Find the numbers and do the arithmetic: 6.1 flowers per plant (alkaloid-free) vs. 2.4 (alkaloid). 2 × 2.4 = 4.8, and 6.1 is bigger than that. Prephrase: they visited a lot more flowers per plant. Watch for answers that swap the two groups.

choices.note: This reverses the groups. The alkaloid-free bees visited more flowers (6.1), not fewer.
CORRECT. 6.1 vs. 2.4 is about two and a half times as many. ‘More than twice’ is exactly right.

Wrong group of facts. On the third paragraph’s worked example, a bee that keeps visiting flowers on one plant leaves mostly the plant’s own pollen on the later flowers, not foreign pollen. This is the opposite.
Wrong group. ‘A sip or two’ describes a bee that tastes the alkaloid (third paragraph). These bees had no alkaloid to taste.
Never stated. Turning to other kinds of flowers is the author’s worry about sparse stands in the last paragraph, and it’s about bees repelled by bitter nectar, not these bees.

questions.stem: In using the phrase ‘to no purpose’ (last paragraph), the author most probably means that the lily’s pollen in such a case
choices: would be carried to lilies too distant to be fertilized by it
would be left on the plant’s own flowers, yielding inbred seeds
would be consumed by the bee instead of being transported
would reach another lily only after its fertility had declined
would be delivered to flowers it cannot fertilize, yielding no lily seeds
questions.explanation: In the last paragraph, a repelled bee in a sparse stand might fly to ‘some other kind of flower altogether,’ so the lily’s pollen would end up on flowers of another species, where it can’t produce lily seeds, which is E. B is tempting because selfing is the other waste the passage discusses, but that happens when a bee stays on one plant, not when it leaves for a different kind of flower.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what ‘to no purpose’ means in its sentence: why would the pollen be wasted?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last paragraph, the sentence about sparse stands and ‘some other kind of flower altogether.’

breakdown.analysis: Read the whole sentence, not just the phrase. In a sparse stand, a bee put off by bitter nectar might go to a different kind of flower, ‘carrying the lily’s pollen to no purpose.’ Why no purpose? Pollen of one species landing on another species’ flower doesn’t make lily seeds. Prephrase: the pollen ends up somewhere it can’t fertilize anything. The passage has two kinds of wasted pollen, and the question is about only one of them.

choices.note: Wrong. The passage never says distance makes a lily unable to be fertilized. The problem in the sentence is the kind of flower, not how far away it is.
Tempting. Selfing is the waste the third paragraph describes. But that happens when the bee stays on the same plant. Here the bee has left for ‘some other kind of flower,’ so this is the wrong waste.
Never mentioned. Nothing in the passage says bees eat the pollen. This is outside knowledge sneaking in.
Invented. The passage says nothing about pollen losing fertility over time.
CORRECT. The bee goes to another kind of flower, so the lily’s pollen lands where it can’t fertilize anything and the lily gets no seeds from it. That’s what ‘to no purpose’ means here.

questions.stem: The primary function of the second paragraph is to
choices: present a reason for doubting a conventional explanation and indicate what kind of explanation must replace it
introduce evidence that the author later uses to argue against the proposal described in the third paragraph
describe the experiment that provides the main support for the explanation that the passage favors
identify an assumption shared by Carrow and by those who hold the thief-deterrence view
qualify the author’s initial endorsement of the view that nectar serves as a payment to pollinators
questions.explanation: The second paragraph gives the usual thief-deterrence answer, undercuts it (ants are scarce and rarely climb the stalks), and concludes that the alkaloid ‘must do’ its work on the bees, which points to the kind of explanation the third paragraph supplies. That is A. C describes the fourth paragraph, not the second, and B gets the direction wrong: the ant evidence supports Carrow rather than being used against her.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what job the second paragraph does in the passage as a whole.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, with a glance at the paragraphs on either side.

breakdown.analysis: Map it: P1 = puzzle. P2 = the usual answer (thieves), a problem with it (few ants, and they don’t climb), and Carrow’s inference: whatever it does, it does to the bees. P3 = Carrow’s actual mechanism. So P2 knocks down the standard answer and narrows the search. Prephrase: it rejects the old explanation and points toward the new one. For function questions, describe the paragraph’s moves in abstract terms and then match.

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘Conventional explanation’ = thief deterrence; ‘reason for doubting’ = scarce ants that rarely climb; ‘what kind of explanation must replace it’ = one about the bees themselves.

Wrong direction. The ant evidence is Carrow’s own point, and it supports her. The author never argues against her proposal; the only reservation (sparse stands) comes in the last paragraph and has nothing to do with ants.
Wrong paragraph. The experiment is in the fourth paragraph. The second has no experiment at all.
Nothing in the paragraph is presented as a shared assumption. It sets the two views against each other.
Wrong. The ‘payment’ idea in the first sentence is background, and the second paragraph doesn’t touch it. Nor is it the author’s ‘endorsement’; it’s how nectar is ‘usually understood.’

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen Carrow’s account of the function of the alkaloid?
choices: Bumblebees that taste the alkaloid at one Varrow lily tend to avoid all Varrow lilies for the remainder of that foraging trip.
The alkaloid is also present in the leaves of the Varrow lily, where it discourages grazing by mammals.
Varrow lilies whose nectar naturally contains little alkaloid have a larger share of seeds that fail to mature than lilies with typical levels.
In laboratory trials, bumblebees offered only alkaloid-laced nectar for several days come to drink it as readily as sweet nectar.
In the stand that Carrow studied, the Varrow lily flowered at the same time as several other plants pollinated by bumblebees.
questions.explanation: Carrow’s chain is: alkaloid → shorter visits → less pollen moved between a plant’s own flowers → fewer inbred seeds that ‘frequently fail.’ C shows that where there is naturally little alkaloid, more seeds fail, which is what the chain predicts in a natural setting rather than a manipulated one. A is the most tempting trap because it sounds like the bitterness working, but a bee that avoids all lilies carries the pollen to no lily at all, which is the waste the author worries about.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that would make Carrow’s explanation (bitter nectar shortens visits and so promotes outcrossing) more believable.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph for the mechanism; fourth for the experiment; last for the worry about bees going elsewhere.

breakdown.analysis: Spell out the chain: 1. Alkaloid → bee leaves after a sip or two. 2. Bee flies on to another lily. 3. Less of the plant’s own pollen moved flower to flower → fewer inbred seeds. 4. Inbred seeds ‘frequently fail,’ so the plant gains. The experiment covered steps 1 and 3. What it didn’t show is that this matters for seed success in plants as they actually grow. We want an answer that links natural alkaloid levels to the payoff. Strengthen answers rarely restate the evidence; they shore up a link the evidence leaves open.

choices.note: Tempting, because it shows bees reacting to the alkaloid. But Carrow needs the bee to go to another lily. If it avoids all lilies for the rest of the trip, the lily’s pollen goes nowhere useful. This hurts step 2.

Tempting as background, but it cuts the wrong way if anything. If the plant makes the alkaloid anyway for its leaves, its presence in nectar might be a side effect rather than something with a pollination job. It doesn’t support Carrow.

CORRECT. Little alkaloid should mean longer visits, more selfing, and more failed seeds. This is that prediction showing up in unmanipulated plants, which ties the alkaloid to an actual benefit for the lily.
Weakens. If bees get used to the bitterness, they would stop leaving early, and the visit-shortening effect would fade.
Irrelevant or slightly damaging. Other bee-pollinated flowers nearby give a departing bee somewhere else to go, which is the author’s worry, not support for Carrow.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the passage?
choices: The alkaloid is present at higher concentrations in Varrow lilies growing in sparse stands than in those growing in dense stands.
Bumblebees cannot detect the alkaloid until they have drunk a substantial amount of nectar containing it.
Draining and refilling the flowers reduced the total number of bee visits that the lilies in Carrow’s experiment received.
Most of the seeds produced by the alkaloid-free plants in Carrow’s experiment failed to develop.
Had bees on alkaloid plants visited as many flowers per plant as bees on alkaloid-free plants, the outcrossing gap would probably have been smaller.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the number of flowers a bee visits on one plant drives how much of the pollen it leaves is the plant’s own, so if visit lengths had been equal, the two groups’ shares of outcrossed seeds (71 vs. 38 percent) should have been closer, which is E. D is the trap: 62 percent of the alkaloid-free plants’ seeds were self-sired, and such seeds ‘frequently fail,’ but ‘frequently’ isn’t ‘mostly,’ so we can’t get to ‘most seeds failed.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the passage backs up best. You may need to combine the mechanism (third paragraph) with the results (fourth).

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third and fourth paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase with five unrelated choices, so test each against the text. The key idea to hold onto: Carrow says the outcrossing difference comes from the visit-length difference. Watch for answers that stretch a number (‘frequently’ into ‘most’) or invent comparisons the passage never makes.

choices.note: Never stated. The passage doesn’t compare alkaloid levels across stands. The sparse-stand discussion is about where bees go, not chemistry.
Contradicted. A bee that tastes the alkaloid ‘takes a sip or two and leaves,’ so bees detect it quickly.
Unknown. Both groups were drained and refilled, so this is the control for that step; the passage gives no total-visit numbers at all.

Tempting. 38 percent outcrossed means 62 percent self-sired, and self-sired seeds ‘frequently fail.’ But ‘frequently fail’ doesn’t mean all or nearly all fail. If, say, half of the self-sired seeds failed, only about 31 percent of all the seeds would fail, not most. Too strong.

CORRECT. The passage’s whole mechanism is that the number of flowers visited per plant drives the share of self pollen. Equalize the visits and you remove the cause of most of the gap, so the difference should shrink. ‘Probably’ keeps it modest.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Hallard is right that Fane’s stage directions are prose fiction, but he is wrong to criticize directors who attempt to stage them.
Hallard’s view that Fane’s directions were meant for readers rather than for productions is poorly supported and fits badly with how Fane used them.
Fane’s stage directions, though long admired by readers, are self-indulgent padding that obscures the theatrical strengths of her plays.
The surviving promptbooks show that Fane expanded her stage directions for readers only after her plays had been performed.
Directors of Fane’s plays should work from the promptbooks of the first productions rather than from the published editions.
questions.explanation: After presenting Hallard’s reading, the author says it fails to clarify what ‘for the reader’ means (second paragraph), relies on an undefended assumption and ambiguous evidence (third), and can’t easily absorb the actors’ recollections (fourth), which is B. A is the half-right trap: the author does defend the directors, but explicitly denies that the directions are ‘fiction for readers.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the one claim the whole passage builds toward.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First sentence of each paragraph: P1 Hallard’s reading; P2 ‘fails to clarify’; P3 ‘relies on an assumption’; P4 ‘a fact Hallard’s account cannot easily absorb.’

breakdown.analysis: This is the classic ‘critic’s view, then what it fails to clarify, the assumption it relies on, and the complication it can’t handle’ structure. The target is Hallard’s reading. So the main point should name Hallard and say his reading falls short. Prephrase: Hallard’s claim that the directions are for readers doesn’t hold up.

choices.note: Half-right trap. The author does hint that the directors understood Fane better than Hallard. But the last paragraph says the directions are ‘neither instructions in the ordinary sense nor fiction for readers.’ The author never grants Hallard’s main claim. Half wrong is all wrong.
CORRECT. It names the target (Hallard’s reading), says it’s poorly supported (P2 and P3), and says it fits poorly with how Fane used the directions (P4, the rehearsal readings).
Wrong party. ‘Self-indulgent padding’ is how earlier critics saw the directions, and the author treats that view as a mistake Hallard improved on.
Too strong, and wrong. The author says the promptbook evidence ‘cuts both ways,’ and the actors’ recollections suggest the full directions existed by the first rehearsal.
Never recommended. The author doesn’t tell directors what to work from. This turns a point about evidence into advice.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward Hallard’s study is most accurately described as
choices: dismissive impatience with its approach
unqualified endorsement of its conclusions
reluctant agreement with its central claim
appreciation tempered by substantial skepticism
detached neutrality regarding its merits
questions.explanation: The author credits Hallard with ‘the merit of taking the directions seriously as writing’ (second paragraph) but then spends the rest of the passage criticizing his reading, which is appreciation tempered by skepticism, D. C is tempting because the author concedes a point, but the author never agrees with Hallard’s central claim that the directions are for readers.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the phrase that matches how the author feels about Hallard’s study: direction and strength.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, first sentence (‘has the merit’), then the criticisms in the second through fourth paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: There’s one compliment (‘has the merit of taking the directions seriously as writing’) and then three paragraphs of criticism in measured language (‘fails to clarify,’ ‘never defends,’ ‘cannot easily absorb’). Prephrase: some credit, mostly doubt. On attitude questions, match both halves of a mixed attitude.

choices.note: Too strong. ‘Dismissive’ ignores the explicit compliment, and the tone is careful, not impatient. The dismissive ones were the earlier critics.
Wrong direction. The author rejects Hallard’s conclusion.

Tempting, because the author does grant Hallard something. But what the author grants is his approach (taking the writing seriously), not his central claim. The author never agrees the directions are for readers.
CORRECT. The ‘merit’ line is the appreciation; the three criticisms are the skepticism. Both halves are in the passage.
Wrong. The author takes clear sides: Hallard’s reading ‘fails to clarify,’ relies on an undefended assumption, and the directors ‘may have understood Fane better than he does.’ That isn’t neutral.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following is true of the details in Fane’s stage directions that specify, for instance, the exact moment a lamp is to dim?
choices: They are among the details that Hallard treats as less central to the directions than their unstageable content.
They were omitted from the promptbooks used in the first productions of Fane’s plays.
They are cited by the author as evidence that Fane wrote her directions for readers.
They were singled out by earlier critics as examples of self-indulgent padding.
They were read aloud to the actors but were not meant to be shown to audiences.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph lists the lamp and the paces as ‘plainly theatrical’ details and says Hallard treats ‘the stageable ones as residue,’ that is, as less central than the unstageable ones, which is A. D is tempting because earlier critics dismissed the directions as padding, but the passage says that of the directions in general, not of these theatrical details.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage actually says about the lamp detail and others like it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, the sentences with ‘plainly theatrical’ and ‘residue.’

breakdown.analysis: The lamp detail is the author’s example of what is ‘plainly theatrical.’ The next sentence says Hallard treats ‘the stageable ones as residue.’ Residue = leftover, not the important part. Prephrase: Hallard downplays these details. Detail questions often hide the answer in a paraphrase: ‘residue’ becomes ‘less central.’

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘Residue’ is the passage’s word for how Hallard treats the stageable details, and the lamp is one of them. ‘Less central than the unstageable content’ is a fair paraphrase.
Never stated. The promptbooks have shorter directions, but the passage doesn’t say which details were cut.
Reversed. The author uses the lamp detail against Hallard: much of what Fane wrote is plainly theatrical, which is a problem for the ‘for readers’ view.

Tempting. Earlier critics called the directions ‘self-indulgent padding,’ but that’s about the directions as a whole. Nothing in the passage says which details the earlier critics had in mind, so this is unsupported.
Mixes up two details. ‘Not meant to be shown’ is said of what a character has never told anyone (fourth paragraph). A lamp dimming is obviously meant to be seen.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: provide evidence that conclusively establishes the view Hallard argues against
describe the publication history of Fane’s plays in order to explain why earlier critics dismissed her directions
identify an undefended assumption behind Hallard’s reading and show that the evidence he cites fits an alternative equally well
concede that the textual history of Fane’s plays supports Hallard’s reading, before turning to considerations that outweigh it
propose a criterion for distinguishing directions written for readers from those written for the stage
questions.explanation: The third paragraph names Hallard’s undefended assumption (a direction can serve a production only by specifying what an audience sees or hears) and then says his promptbook evidence ‘cuts both ways,’ being equally consistent with an alternative, which is C. D is the trap: the author says the evidence is consistent with Hallard’s reading but ‘equally consistent’ with another, so it doesn’t concede that the evidence supports Hallard on balance.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what job the third paragraph does in the argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, especially ‘an assumption Hallard never defends’ and ‘that evidence cuts both ways.’

breakdown.analysis: Two moves: 1. Name Hallard’s hidden assumption (serving a production = specifying something seen or heard). 2. Take his evidence (printed directions longer than promptbooks) and show it fits an alternative story just as well. Prephrase: expose an assumption and neutralize his evidence. Watch for answers that turn ‘equally consistent’ into ‘supports’ or ‘refutes.’

choices.note: Too strong. The paragraph says the evidence ‘cuts both ways.’ Nothing here is conclusive, and Hallard isn’t arguing against a named view.
Wrong purpose. The earlier critics appear in the second paragraph, and nothing in the third explains their dismissal.
CORRECT. Both moves are here: the undefended assumption, then the point that the promptbook evidence fits the alternative ‘equally.’ Evidence that fits two stories equally doesn’t favor either.

Tempting, because the author does say the evidence ‘is consistent with’ Hallard’s view. But ‘equally consistent’ with the alternative means it doesn’t support him on balance. This isn’t a concede-then-outweigh paragraph.
Wrong. The second paragraph complains that Hallard never clarifies this distinction; the author doesn’t supply a criterion either, here or anywhere.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the detail concerning what a character ‘has never told anyone and never will’ (first paragraph)?
choices: It is an example of the stageable material that Hallard treats as residue.
It shows that Fane intended at least some of her directions to be read only by readers of her published plays.
It was probably added to the published text of The Glass Orchard after the play’s premiere.
It should be conveyed to audiences through some means other than the characters’ dialogue.
It can serve a purpose in performance even though nothing in a production directly represents it.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the detail ‘was not meant to be shown’ but ‘to be known by the actor, and to shape everything she did onstage,’ so it serves performance without being represented, which is E. D is the most tempting trap because the detail does seem to need some outlet, but the author says it was not meant to be shown to the audience at all; it works through the actor.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the author would say about the ‘never told anyone’ detail.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, ‘was not meant to be shown; it was meant to be known by the actor’; also the third paragraph’s rejected assumption.

breakdown.analysis: Is an unstageable detail useless onstage? Hallard’s assumption says yes: a direction serves a production only by specifying something the audience sees or hears. The author rejects that, and the fourth paragraph gives the example: this detail isn’t shown, but the actor knows it and it shapes everything she does. Prephrase: it helps the performance without ever appearing in it.

choices.note: Wrong category. A secret a character will never tell is the clearest unstageable detail in the passage. The stageable ones are the lamp and the paces.
That’s Hallard’s conclusion, not the author’s. The author suggests the opposite: it was for the actor.
Unsupported, and the fourth paragraph points the other way: Fane read ‘the full directions’ aloud at the first rehearsal, so the long directions existed before the premiere.

Tempting, because it sounds like a reasonable stage practice. But the author says the detail ‘was not meant to be shown’; it’s meant to be known by the actor. The passage says nothing about conveying it to audiences by any route.
CORRECT. Not represented (‘not meant to be shown’), but it serves the performance (it ‘shape[s] everything she did onstage’). This is exactly the possibility Hallard’s assumption rules out.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the use of stage directions that the actors’ recollections (last paragraph) attribute to Fane?
choices: Before rehearsals, a choreographer tells the dancers an imagined life story for each character, never mentions it again, and depicts none of it in the dance.
A composer publishes a score with detailed performance markings that the musicians are expected to consult at every rehearsal.
A novelist adapting her novel for the stage cuts every descriptive passage that could not be shown to an audience.
A film director writes notes on each scene for a book published after the film’s release, intended for readers curious about the production.
At the first rehearsal, a playwright gives the actors a summary of the plot so that they can learn their lines more quickly.
questions.explanation: Fane read the full directions aloud once, at the start, never referred to them again, and their unstageable content was meant to shape the actors’ work without being shown, which matches the choreographer’s one-time briefing on undepicted life stories in A. E is the closest trap: it has the one-time briefing at the first rehearsal, but the plot is what the play shows, and the purpose is learning lines, not shaping performance with hidden knowledge.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the situation that works the way Fane’s use of her directions worked, as the actors describe it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph: ‘read the full directions aloud at the first rehearsal... and never referred to them again’; ‘not meant to be shown... meant to be known by the actor.’

breakdown.analysis: List the features: 1. The creator conveys material once, at the start. 2. Never referred to again. 3. Much of it is never shown to the audience. 4. It still shapes the performers’ work. The right answer needs all four. Analogy answers share structure, not subject matter.

choices.note: CORRECT. One telling before rehearsals, never mentioned again, undepicted, and meant to inform how the dancers play the characters. All four features match.

Wrong. Consulting the markings at every rehearsal is the opposite of ‘never referred to them again,’ and performance markings are ordinary instructions, which the author says Fane’s directions are not.
Wrong. Cutting what can’t be shown is the opposite of Fane, who kept unstageable material and gave it to the actors.
This matches Hallard’s picture (written for readers, after the fact), not the actors’ recollections.

Tempting: the one-time briefing at the first rehearsal matches. But a plot summary covers what the play will show, and its job is memorization. Fane’s directions carried things not shown, meant to shape how the actors played their parts. Half a match isn’t enough.

questions.stem: The author’s view of the evidence Hallard draws from the promptbooks (third paragraph) is most accurately described by which one of the following?
choices: It undermines Hallard’s reading, because the promptbooks reflect the involvement of Fane herself in the first productions.
It favors Hallard’s reading, but only slightly, because few promptbooks from the first productions survive.
It has no bearing on Fane’s intentions, because the promptbooks record the choices of directors rather than those of Fane.
It is as compatible with Fane’s having conveyed the fuller directions to performers by other means as with Hallard’s reading.
It establishes that Fane lengthened her directions after the premieres, a fact that Hallard’s reading cannot accommodate.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the promptbook evidence ‘cuts both ways’: it is consistent with Fane’s having expanded the directions for readers and ‘equally consistent’ with her having set down in print what she conveyed to performers by other means, which is D. E is the strongest trap, since printed directions longer than promptbook ones seem to show later expansion, but the fourth paragraph says Fane read ‘the full directions’ at the first rehearsal, and in any case later expansion would fit Hallard, not defeat him. A is tempting because the author opposes Hallard, but the author does not treat this evidence as counting against him.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say exactly how much weight, and in which direction, the author gives the promptbook evidence.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, last three sentences (‘Hallard cites... cuts both ways... equally consistent’); fourth paragraph, the first-rehearsal reading.

breakdown.analysis: Does the promptbook evidence help Hallard or hurt him? Neither, says the author: ‘that evidence cuts both ways.’ It fits Hallard’s story (Fane expanded the directions for readers) and ‘equally’ fits the other story (she wrote down in print what she had already passed on to the actors another way). Evidence that fits two stories equally doesn’t favor either. Prephrase: neutral; compatible with both. The author does favor the alternative, but the reason is the actors’ recollections in the fourth paragraph, not the promptbooks. Don’t let the author’s overall side leak into a question about one piece of evidence.

choices.note: Tempting, since the author is against Hallard and mentions Fane’s involvement. But the author never says the evidence undermines Hallard; it ‘cuts both ways.’ The overall verdict is being pinned on the wrong piece of evidence.
Wrong on both counts. ‘Equally consistent’ means it doesn’t favor Hallard even slightly, and the passage never says how many promptbooks survive.
Contradicted. The passage says Fane was ‘closely involved’ in these productions, and the author treats the evidence as relevant; it just doesn’t pick a side.

CORRECT. This is the ‘cuts both ways’ sentence in other words: consistent with Hallard’s reading, and ‘equally consistent’ with Fane’s having set down in print what she had conveyed to performers by other means.

Strong trap. Longer printed directions feel like proof of later expansion. But the author says the evidence is only consistent with expansion, and the fourth paragraph has Fane reading ‘the full directions’ at the first rehearsal. Besides, expansion for readers is Hallard’s story, so it would hardly be a fact his reading ‘cannot accommodate.’ Two errors in one choice.

questions.stimulus: Literary critic: For most of the last century, poets from the Varden region wrote almost exclusively in rhymed, metered forms, and many readers still associate the region's poetry with those forms. Some critics now claim that the younger Varden poets who write in free verse have abandoned their tradition. But these poets draw their imagery from the same rivers, harvests, and village festivals their predecessors did, and they often quote older Varden poems directly. A tradition lives in its subjects and its memory as much as in its forms. So the younger poets are carrying the Varden tradition forward, not abandoning it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the literary critic's argument?
choices: For most of the last century, Varden poets wrote almost exclusively in rhymed, metered forms.
A literary tradition consists more in its subjects and its memory than in its forms.
The younger Varden poets who write in free verse are carrying their region's poetic tradition forward.
The critics who say the younger Varden poets have abandoned their tradition are relying on readers' associations.
The younger Varden poets often quote older Varden poems directly.
questions.explanation: The critic rejects the claim that the free-verse poets have abandoned the tradition and concludes, in the last sentence, that they are carrying it forward (C); the opening sentence is background and the middle sentences are support. B is the tempting distortion: the critic says a tradition lives in its subjects and memory 'as much as' in its forms, not 'more,' and that general claim is a premise anyway.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The younger free-verse Varden poets are carrying the tradition forward, not abandoning it.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: They use the same imagery as their predecessors; they quote older Varden poems; a tradition lives in its subjects and memory as much as in its forms.

breakdown.analysis: What is the critic trying to prove? Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The first sentence is just background (the history of rhymed forms) and you can ignore it. The second sentence is the view the critic opposes. The imagery, the quoting, and the general claim about traditions all point to one thing: the young poets aren't abandoning the tradition. That's the last sentence, flagged by 'So.'

choices.note: Background. It sets the scene for why some critics think free verse is a break. It supports nothing and isn't the point.
