Tempting, because it's the general principle the argument leans on. But it's a premise, not the conclusion, and it's distorted: the critic says 'as much as,' not 'more than.'
CORRECT. This is the 'So' sentence, and the imagery, the quoting, and the principle about traditions are all offered in support of it.
The critic never says why the opposing critics think what they do. This invents a diagnosis of the opponents.
A premise. It's one of the pieces of evidence that the young poets keep the tradition alive.

questions.stimulus: Parent: Child psychologists claim that toddlers who are read to every day go on to develop larger vocabularies than toddlers who are not. But my neighbor read to her son every night from the time he was born, and at age three he still spoke fewer words than most children his age. Clearly, the psychologists have overstated the benefits of reading to toddlers.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the parent's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: treats a single counterexample as sufficient grounds for rejecting a claim about a general tendency
presumes, without providing justification, that reading aloud is the only way to build a toddler's vocabulary
relies on the report of a neighbor who is not an expert in child development
fails to consider that toddlers who are read to may also be spoken to more often by their parents
takes for granted that a child's vocabulary at age three predicts the size of his vocabulary later in life
questions.explanation: The psychologists' claim is about a general tendency, and one child who doesn't fit it does nothing to show the tendency is overstated, so A describes the flaw. C is tempting, but the neighbor is reporting simple facts about her own son (how often she read, how many words he says), which needs no expertise; the problem is drawing a general conclusion from one case.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Psychologists have overstated the benefits of reading to toddlers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: One neighbor read to her son nightly, and at three he spoke fewer words than most kids his age.

breakdown.analysis: So one kid didn't fit the pattern. So what? The psychologists made a claim about toddlers in general: on average, the ones read to every day end up with bigger vocabularies. A general tendency survives plenty of exceptions. It's like arguing: my uncle smoked every day and lived to 95, so doctors exaggerate the risks of smoking. That's the anecdote-versus-general-claim flaw. It's a classic; know it. We need an answer that says the parent used one case to reject a claim about a group.

choices.note: CORRECT. One child who didn't benefit can't show that reading's average benefit is overstated.
The parent never says or assumes reading is the only way. If anything, the neighbor's son shows other things matter too.
choices.example: Example of flaw: My daughter's vocabulary is small, so she must not have been read to enough.

choices.note: Tempting, because it names an authority problem. But the neighbor isn't offering an expert opinion. She's reporting how often she read and how many words her son uses, which anyone can know. The issue is that it's only one child.
choices.example: Example of flaw: My neighbor, who isn't a doctor, says this vitamin cures colds, so it does.

choices.note: This is a possible problem with the psychologists' causal claim, not with the parent's reasoning. The parent's mistake is the leap from one case to a general rejection.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Kids who are read to have big vocabularies, so reading causes big vocabularies (ignoring that those kids are also talked to more).

choices.note: The parent doesn't need this. The parent's claim is about the son at age three, and the conclusion fails for a different reason: one case can't overturn a trend.
choices.example: Example of flaw: He was slow to talk at three, so he'll always have a small vocabulary.

questions.stimulus: Primatologist: In the Kessa Forest, groups of capuchin monkeys in which members spend more time grooming one another have fewer violent conflicts within the group than other groups do. Grooming, then, must reduce tension among group members and thereby prevent conflict.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the primatologist's argument?
choices: Capuchin groups in several other forests also spend a large share of their time grooming one another.
Grooming also helps capuchins remove ticks and other parasites from one another's fur.
Some violent conflicts within capuchin groups occur between monkeys that groomed each other earlier the same day.
Capuchins rarely groom group members with whom they have recently fought, and in groups where fights are frequent, few pairs of monkeys remain on friendly terms.
The Kessa Forest groups that groom the most are, on average, no larger than the groups that groom the least.
questions.explanation: The argument infers that grooming prevents conflict from a correlation between the two. D suggests the causation runs the other way: frequent fighting leaves few friendly pairs, so conflict suppresses grooming. C is tempting but only shows that grooming doesn't prevent every conflict, which is consistent with its reducing conflict overall; E, by ruling out group size as a factor, actually helps the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Grooming reduces tension and so prevents conflict.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Groups that groom more have fewer violent conflicts.

breakdown.analysis: Groups that groom a lot fight less. But which way does the arrow point? Maybe groups that fight less have more friends to groom. It's like saying couples who hold hands argue less, so holding hands prevents arguments; maybe couples who don't argue just feel like holding hands. We need an answer that shows the correlation could come from conflict reducing grooming (reverse causation) or from a third factor.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Grooming elsewhere tells us nothing about whether grooming causes fewer fights in Kessa.
So? Grooming can have more than one function. Removing parasites doesn't stop it from also reducing tension.
Tempting. It shows grooming doesn't prevent every fight. But the claim is that grooming reduces conflict, not that it eliminates it. A few exceptions barely dent that.

CORRECT. This reverses the arrow. Fighting kills friendships, and monkeys don't groom the ones they've been fighting with. So high-conflict groups would groom less even if grooming did nothing to prevent conflict.
This strengthens. It rules out group size as a hidden factor behind both grooming and conflict.

questions.stimulus: In the Marro Valley, farmers who stopped plowing their fields and instead planted directly into the previous year's crop residue found that, within a few years, their soil held considerably more water after a rain. Yet in years with cool, wet springs, these farmers' fields produced smaller harvests than plowed fields did.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Plowed fields in the Marro Valley lose more topsoil to erosion than unplowed fields do.
The layer of crop residue on unplowed fields keeps the soil from warming in spring, and seeds germinate poorly in cold, waterlogged soil.
Most Marro Valley farmers who stopped plowing did so in order to reduce their fuel costs.
In years with hot, dry summers, unplowed fields in the Marro Valley produce larger harvests than plowed fields do.
Soil that holds more water after a rain generally supports a larger population of earthworms.
questions.explanation: Holding more water sounds like a pure benefit, yet the unplowed fields do worse in cool, wet springs. B explains this: the residue keeps the soil cold, and wet, cold soil is bad for germination, so the extra moisture becomes a liability in exactly those springs. D is tempting because it is about yields, but it describes dry years and only adds to the puzzle about wet ones.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Unplowed fields hold more water after rain, but in cool, wet springs they yield less than plowed fields.

breakdown.analysis: Why would better water-holding soil lose out? Notice the specific years: cool and wet. In those years, extra water isn't helping anyone. We need an answer that shows something about unplowed fields that hurts crops specifically when springs are cool and wet.

choices.note: This is another advantage of not plowing. It makes the lower yields more puzzling, not less.
CORRECT. In cool, wet springs the residue keeps the soil cold, and cold, soggy soil means poor germination. The unplowed fields' extra water and the residue both hurt in exactly those years.
Why farmers switched doesn't explain how the fields perform.
Tempting, because it's about harvests. But it covers hot, dry years, where you'd expect water-holding soil to win. It says nothing about the cool, wet springs that need explaining.
Another apparent benefit of moist soil. Nothing here explains a lower harvest.

questions.stimulus: Hospital administrator: Last year our hospital hired additional night-shift nurses for its surgical ward. This year, the ward recorded a third fewer patient falls than it did the year before. So hiring the additional nurses reduced the number of falls on the ward.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the administrator's argument?
choices: Most of the patient falls on the surgical ward occur during the night shift.
No other hospital in the region reduced its number of patient falls without hiring additional nurses.
The additional nurses hired last year were more experienced than the nurses already working on the ward.
Patient falls are the most serious safety problem on the hospital's surgical ward.
Not all of this year's reduction in falls on the ward would have occurred even if the additional nurses had not been hired.
questions.explanation: To credit the hiring with the drop in falls, the administrator must assume the drop would not have happened anyway; E states exactly that in modest form, and if it were false (the whole reduction would have occurred regardless) the hiring reduced nothing. A is tempting, but negating it (fewer than half of the falls occur at night) leaves room for the new night nurses to prevent some falls.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Hiring the additional night-shift nurses reduced falls on the surgical ward.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The nurses were hired last year; this year falls dropped by a third.

breakdown.analysis: Falls dropped after the hiring. Would they have dropped anyway? Maybe fewer surgeries, a new bed design, or a lucky year. Structure: 1. Nurses hired. 2. Falls down a third. → The hiring caused the drop. Crediting an action for an outcome needs the outcome not to have happened anyway. We need an answer that says: without the nurses, at least some of the reduction wouldn't have happened. Negate each choice.

choices.note: Tempting, since these are night nurses. But negate it: fewer than half of falls are at night. Night falls still happen, and the new nurses could have prevented some of them. Argument survives.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most of the ward's falls occur during the night shift.

choices.note: Other hospitals are irrelevant. Even if some hospital cut falls another way, our hiring could still have worked here.
choices.negation: Some other hospital in the region reduced its falls without hiring additional nurses.

choices.note: Not required. New nurses of equal experience could still help simply by being extra hands.
choices.negation: The additional nurses were not more experienced than the existing nurses.

choices.note: Unsupported ranking, and irrelevant. Whether falls are the worst problem doesn't affect whether the hiring reduced them.
choices.negation: Patient falls are not the most serious safety problem on the ward.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the entire reduction would have happened even without the new nurses. Then the hiring reduced nothing, and the conclusion collapses. Note the modest 'not all' wording, typical of required assumptions.
choices.negation: All of this year's reduction in falls would have occurred even if the additional nurses had not been hired.

questions.stimulus: Energy analyst: In the Corran electricity market, wholesale prices during evening hours have fallen sharply since several large battery storage facilities began operating two years ago. These facilities charge their batteries at midday, when abundant solar generation makes electricity cheap, and sell the stored power in the evening. So the battery facilities are responsible for the drop in evening prices.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the energy analyst's argument?
choices: Over the past two years, evening demand for electricity in the Corran market has not declined, and no other new sources of evening supply have begun operating there.
Battery storage facilities have also been built in several other electricity markets over the past two years.
Several of the battery storage facilities in the Corran market are owned by companies that also own solar farms.
Evening wholesale prices in the Corran market were higher three years ago than they had been five years ago.
Consumers in the Corran market use more electricity during evening hours than during midday hours.
questions.explanation: The analyst attributes the fall in evening prices to the batteries, so the argument is strengthened by ruling out other explanations; A eliminates the two most obvious ones, falling demand and new supply. E is tempting because it explains why evening power is valuable, but it gives no reason to think the batteries rather than something else caused the price drop.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The battery facilities caused the drop in evening wholesale prices.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Evening prices fell after the batteries started; batteries buy cheap midday power and sell it in the evening.

breakdown.analysis: Prices fell after the batteries arrived. Could something else have pushed them down? Prices drop when demand falls or supply rises from some other source. If either happened, the batteries might deserve little credit. We need an answer that rules out those alternatives. Strengtheners often work this way: they don't prove the cause, they knock out rivals.

choices.note: CORRECT. It rules out the two obvious alternatives: demand didn't drop, and no other new supply came in. That leaves the batteries as the best explanation for cheaper evening power.
Irrelevant. Other markets having batteries tells us nothing unless we know what happened to their prices.
Who owns the batteries doesn't affect whether they lowered prices.
Old history from before the batteries existed. It doesn't bear on why prices fell in the last two years.
Tempting, since it shows evening power matters. But it's background, not evidence that the batteries rather than some other factor caused the drop.

questions.stimulus: Art dealer: Collectors and critics agree that the Halden Group, a circle of painters active in the 1920s, produced some of the most important art of its era. This small still life is signed by Otto Brenk, who was a member of the Halden Group. The still life is therefore an important work.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the art dealer's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: relies on the opinions of collectors, whose judgments may be influenced by market prices
takes for granted that a painting's importance depends on when it was painted
presumes that because a group of painters produced important work, each work by a member of the group is important
fails to consider that the signature on the still life might have been forged
confuses the importance of an artwork with its value on the art market
questions.explanation: The dealer moves from a claim about the group's output as a whole to a claim about one particular painting by one member, a part/whole error described in C. D is tempting because a forged signature would also undermine the conclusion, but the argument's reasoning would be flawed even if the signature were genuine; a merely possible fact is not the flaw in the reasoning.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: This Brenk still life is an important work.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The Halden Group produced some of the era's most important art; Brenk was a member.

breakdown.analysis: The group produced important art. Does that make every painting by every member important? No. 'Some of the most important art' could have come from two or three members' best works, while Brenk painted forgettable still lifes. It's like saying the team won the championship, so its backup goalie must be great. That's a part/whole error (division): what's true of the whole isn't automatically true of each part. Worth knowing. We need an answer that names that move.

choices.note: The argument does lean on collectors and critics, but the problem isn't their motives. Even if their judgment is perfect, it's about the group, not this painting.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Collectors say this artist is great, but collectors just want prices to rise, so she isn't.

choices.note: The argument never ties importance to date. The 1920s is just when the group was active.
choices.example: Example of flaw: This painting is from the 1920s, the golden age, so it must be important.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the jump from the group's importance to the importance of one work by one member.

Tempting, because a forgery would sink the conclusion. But that's merely possible; nothing suggests it. And even with a genuine signature, the reasoning still fails. You can't pick an answer on a possibility the argument doesn't depend on.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The painting has a Brenk signature, so Brenk definitely painted it.

choices.note: The dealer never mentions price or market value.
choices.example: Example of flaw: This painting sold for a fortune, so it must be artistically important.

questions.stimulus: At Tarrant Freight, a shipment may be sent by express air only if the customer has prepaid the express surcharge for it. Any shipment containing lithium batteries must travel by sea unless it has been inspected by a certified handler. No shipment travels both by express air and by sea. Last week, a shipment for the customer Holloway contained lithium batteries and was sent by express air.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Holloway's shipment did not travel by sea, and it was not inspected by a certified handler.
Every shipment at Tarrant Freight that has been inspected by a certified handler is sent by express air.
Holloway has prepaid the express surcharge on every shipment it has sent through Tarrant Freight.
Every shipment at Tarrant Freight for which the express surcharge was prepaid was sent by express air.
Holloway's shipment was inspected by a certified handler, and Holloway prepaid the express surcharge for it.
questions.explanation: Express air requires a prepaid surcharge, so Holloway prepaid it; and since the shipment went by air it did not go by sea, so the lithium-battery shipment must have been inspected (otherwise it would have had to go by sea). E combines both results. D reverses the first rule, and C stretches a fact about one shipment to all of Holloway's shipments.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Express air → surcharge prepaid; 2. Lithium AND not inspected → by sea; 3. Not both air and sea; 4. Holloway's shipment: lithium, sent by express air.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. From 4 and 1: express air → prepaid. So Holloway prepaid. From 4 and 3: air → not sea. Rule 2's contrapositive: not sea → not lithium OR inspected. The shipment had lithium, so it was inspected. Two firm results: prepaid and inspected. Watch for answers that reverse a rule or stretch one shipment into 'every.'

choices.note: Half right, half opposite. It didn't go by sea, but it must have been inspected, or it would have had to go by sea.
Reverses the logic. Inspection removes the must-go-by-sea requirement; it doesn't send anything by air.
Too broad. We know about one shipment, not every shipment Holloway has ever sent.
This reverses rule 1. Prepaying is required for express air, not a guarantee of it.
CORRECT. Express air → prepaid. Express air → not sea → (since it has lithium) inspected. Both halves are forced.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: The Alvaro Foundation recently sold a painting from its collection to raise money for its art-education programs. The painting was donated decades ago by a collector who expressed no wishes about whether it could ever be sold, and the money from the sale will fund programs that serve the foundation's stated mission. Some members of the public object to the sale, but the foundation acted properly.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?
choices: An institution should never sell a donated work while members of the public object to the sale.
An institution acts properly in selling a donated work if the donor placed no restriction on its sale and the proceeds are used to advance the institution's mission.
An institution acts properly whenever most members of the public support its decisions about its collection.
If the proceeds from selling a donated work are used for purposes outside an institution's mission, the sale is improper.
A donor who expresses no wishes about a gift's future gives up any claim to control how the gift is used.
questions.explanation: The ethicist concludes the sale was proper because the donor set no restriction and the proceeds serve the mission; B says exactly those two conditions make a sale proper. D is tempting because it mentions the mission, but it only says when a sale is improper, so it can never establish that this sale was proper; E covers the donor condition but says nothing about whether the sale was proper.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The foundation acted properly in selling the painting.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The donor set no wishes about selling it; the proceeds fund programs that serve the foundation's mission.

breakdown.analysis: Two facts, one verdict: proper. What rule turns those facts into that verdict? A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. We need: no donor restriction AND proceeds serve the mission → selling is proper.

choices.note: Opposite direction. This would condemn the sale, since some members of the public object.
CORRECT. Both conditions match the facts (no restriction, mission-serving proceeds), and the rule delivers the exact conclusion: proper.
We don't know what most of the public thinks, and the ethicist doesn't rely on popularity.
Tempting, since it mentions the mission. But it only tells you when a sale is improper. Avoiding that condition doesn't make a sale proper. That's the sufficient/necessary mix-up in principle form.
Covers only the donor half, and stops short of the verdict. Even if the donor gave up control, that doesn't say the sale was proper (what if the money were wasted?).

questions.stimulus: Editor: Some anthology editors propose that a poem be included in a school anthology only if it was widely read in its own time. But many poems now regarded as central to the literary canon found few readers when they were first published. If the proposal were adopted, then, school anthologies would have to omit many of the very poems that students most need to know. Editors should therefore reject the proposal.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the editor's argument by the claim that school anthologies would have to omit many of the very poems that students most need to know?
choices: It is the main conclusion of the editor's argument.
It is offered as support for the claim that many canonical poems found few readers when first published.
It is a claim the editor attributes to the anthology editors who favor the proposal.
It is an unacceptable consequence that, according to the editor, would follow from adopting the proposal.
It is a general principle that the editor uses to evaluate proposals about school anthologies.
questions.explanation: The editor derives this result from the proposal (via the fact that many canonical poems were little read at first) and uses it as the reason to reject the proposal, so it is an unwelcome consequence of adopting the proposal (D). A is tempting because the claim is itself supported, but it serves as support for the final sentence, the recommendation to reject the proposal, which is the main conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Editors should reject the proposal.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Many canonical poems had few readers at first; so under the proposal, anthologies would have to omit many poems students most need; that result is unacceptable.

breakdown.analysis: Does the editor want anthologies to omit those poems? Of course not. The editor doesn't believe this should happen. It's the bad result used to sink the rule. Structure: 1. Proposal: include only poems widely read in their time. 2. Many canonical poems weren't. → 3. Adopting the proposal would cut those poems. → Reject the proposal. The statement in question is step 3: a consequence of the proposal that the editor treats as unacceptable.

choices.note: Tempting, since the claim is supported by the line before it. But it's then used to support the last sentence. The main conclusion is 'reject the proposal.'
Reversed. The claim about canonical poems supports this statement, not the other way around.
The proposal's supporters would never say this; it's the editor's own objection to their proposal.
CORRECT. The editor derives it from the proposal and treats it as unacceptable, which is the reason to reject the proposal.
It's not a general principle. It's a specific prediction about what this proposal would do.

questions.stimulus: Child development researcher: We asked the parents of 400 kindergartners how often their children engaged in unstructured, imaginative play at home. The children whose parents reported the most imaginative play scored highest, on average, on a test of self-control given at school. Thus, imaginative play helps young children develop self-control.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the researcher's argument?
choices: Children who already have good self-control are better able to sustain long imaginative games and so tend to spend more time playing them.
Some of the children whose parents reported little imaginative play also scored well on the test of self-control.
The test of self-control used in the study has also been given to kindergartners in several other countries.
Imaginative play has also been found to help young children develop larger vocabularies.
The parents in the study were not told in advance that their children would be given a test of self-control.
questions.explanation: The researcher infers that play builds self-control from a correlation between them. A gives the reverse explanation: self-control makes children better at, and so more drawn to, sustained imaginative play. B is tempting, but a few exceptions are fully compatible with an average effect.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Imaginative play helps children develop self-control.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Kids whose parents reported the most imaginative play scored highest on a self-control test.

breakdown.analysis: More play goes with more self-control. But which comes first? Maybe kids who can already sit still and stay with a game are the ones who play long make-believe games. Correlation alone can't tell you the direction. We need an answer that offers reverse causation or a third factor.

choices.note: CORRECT. Reverse causation. If self-control leads to more imaginative play, the correlation would show up even if play builds no self-control at all.
Tempting. But 'some' exceptions don't undercut an average. The study only claimed that high-play kids scored highest on average.
Irrelevant. Where else the test has been used says nothing about cause here.
So? Play can have more than one benefit. This doesn't touch the self-control claim.
If anything this mildly helps, since parents couldn't tailor their reports to the test. It doesn't weaken.

questions.stimulus: Soil scientist: When farmers apply more nitrogen fertilizer than their crops can absorb, the excess acidifies the soil, harms beneficial soil microbes, and washes into nearby streams as nitrate. Farmers who care about the long-term health of their soil, therefore, should not apply nitrogen fertilizer to their fields at all.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the soil scientist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to consider that some farmers may not care about the long-term health of their soil
draws a conclusion about soil health from evidence that concerns only the health of streams
confuses a condition that is necessary for healthy soil with one that is sufficient for it
takes for granted that harm to soil microbes is more serious than harm to streams
takes for granted that what is harmful in excessive amounts is harmful in any amount
questions.explanation: The evidence concerns only fertilizer beyond what crops can absorb, yet the conclusion rules out applying any nitrogen fertilizer; E names that leap from excess to any amount. B is tempting because streams are mentioned, but the scientist also cites soil acidification and harm to microbes, so the evidence is not only about streams.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Soil-conscious farmers should apply no nitrogen fertilizer at all.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Fertilizer beyond what crops can absorb acidifies soil, harms microbes, and pollutes streams.

breakdown.analysis: Too much fertilizer is harmful. Does that mean any fertilizer is harmful? Read the first sentence closely: the damage comes from the excess, the part crops can't absorb. Apply only what the crop takes up and, as far as we're told, there's no excess. It's like saying too much water drowns houseplants, so never water your plants. That's the 'excess is harmful, so never use any' flaw. We need an answer that names that jump.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The conclusion is limited to farmers who do care about soil health, so other farmers don't matter.
choices.example: Example of flaw: All farmers want healthy soil, so every farmer will follow this advice.

choices.note: Tempting, since streams come up. But two of the three harms (acidification, microbes) are about soil. The evidence isn't only about streams.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Fertilizer pollutes streams, so it must damage soil too.

choices.note: No necessary or sufficient condition for healthy soil is stated or confused here. Sounds technical, but it doesn't fit.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Healthy soil requires microbes; this soil has microbes; so it's healthy.

choices.note: The argument never ranks the harms. It lists them together.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Fertilizer harms microbes more than streams, so we should worry only about microbes.

choices.note: CORRECT. The evidence is about amounts beyond what crops absorb; the conclusion bans every amount.

questions.stimulus: Many people believe that the hospitals with the longest emergency-room waits are the worst managed. But wait times depend heavily on how many patients arrive, and hospitals with strong reputations tend to attract patients from well beyond their own neighborhoods. Moreover, a well-run emergency room treats the most urgent cases first, which lengthens the waits of patients with minor complaints. So a long average wait at a hospital's emergency room ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: is a reliable sign that the emergency room is poorly managed
results mainly from the emergency room's failure to treat the most urgent cases first
is not, by itself, good evidence that the emergency room is poorly managed
shows that the hospital has the strongest reputation in its region
could be eliminated if emergency rooms stopped treating the most urgent cases first
questions.explanation: The author pushes back on the popular view by giving two reasons a long wait can coexist with, or even reflect, good management (a strong reputation drawing patients, and treating urgent cases first). The fitting conclusion is the modest C. A repeats the popular view the author is rejecting, and D overstates what a long wait shows.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Popular view: longest waits = worst managed; 2. Waits depend on patient volume, and well-regarded hospitals draw more patients; 3. Good ERs treat urgent cases first, lengthening minor-case waits.

breakdown.analysis: The 'But' tells you the author disagrees with the popular view. Both reasons point the same way: a long wait can come from things that go with good management. So the blank should say long waits don't prove bad management. Watch for the trap that repeats the popular view, and for answers that swing too far the other way.

choices.note: This is the popular view the author just argued against. Classic trap: it echoes the first sentence.
Opposite. The author says good ERs do treat urgent cases first, and that this is part of why waits are long.
CORRECT. Modest and exactly what both reasons support: long waits have innocent (even good) explanations, so they don't show poor management on their own.
Too strong. A strong reputation is one possible cause of long waits, and 'strongest in its region' is a ranking nothing supports.
The author presents treating urgent cases first as good practice. Nothing suggests abandoning it, and it wouldn't eliminate waits anyway.

questions.stimulus: Every macaque troop on Pemba Ridge that forages in the farmers' orchards has learned to raid storage sheds. No troop that has learned to raid storage sheds is left unmonitored by the wildlife service. So any troop on Pemba Ridge that the wildlife service leaves unmonitored does not forage in the farmers' orchards.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Every poem in the Larkin collection that was written before 1950 uses rhyme. No poem that uses rhyme was chosen for the festival reading. So any poem in the collection that was chosen for the festival reading was written before 1950.

Every tenant in the Morrow Building who has a pet has signed the pet agreement. No tenant who has signed the pet agreement is exempt from the cleaning fee. So any tenant in the Morrow Building who is exempt from the cleaning fee does not have a pet.

Every student in Ms. Ortega's class who completed the reading passed the quiz. Some students who passed the quiz did not attend the review session. So some student in the class who completed the reading did not attend the review session.

Every vehicle in the city fleet that runs on diesel is inspected annually. Every vehicle that is inspected annually is kept in the north garage. So every diesel vehicle in the city fleet is kept in the north garage.

No apprentice in the Garvey workshop is permitted to use the lathe. Every worker who is permitted to use the lathe has completed safety training. So no apprentice in the workshop has completed safety training.
questions.explanation: The argument runs: all A are B; no B is C; so any C is not A (a valid chain stated in contrapositive form). B matches term for term: pet owners sign the agreement, no signer is exempt, so any exempt tenant has no pet. D is tempting because it is also a valid all-all chain, but it has no 'no' premise and does not conclude in contrapositive form; A and E are invalid.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Any unmonitored troop doesn't forage in the orchards.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Forages in orchards → raids sheds; raids sheds → monitored (not unmonitored).

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A → B; B → not C; so C → not A. (Valid; conclusion in contrapositive form.)

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: orchards → sheds → monitored. Contrapositive: unmonitored → no sheds → no orchards. Valid. So we need a valid argument with the same shape: an 'every' premise, a 'no' premise, and a conclusion that starts from the 'no' group and denies the first group.

choices.note: Rhyme → not chosen. So pre-1950 → not chosen. The argument concludes the reverse (chosen → pre-1950), which doesn't follow. Invalid.
CORRECT. Pet → signed → not exempt. Contrapositive: exempt → not signed → no pet. Same terms in the same order, same contrapositive conclusion.
Uses 'some' and concludes something that doesn't follow (the students who skipped could be ones who didn't do the reading). Different and invalid.
Tempting: a valid two-step chain. But it's all-all-all with a forward conclusion. No 'no' premise, no contrapositive conclusion.
Apprentice → no lathe; lathe → training. Nothing follows about apprentices and training. Invalid.

questions.stimulus: Regulator: The Dunmore Power Company has asked permission to raise its residential electricity rates, citing recent increases in fuel prices. But Dunmore buys all of its electricity from other companies under long-term contracts that fix the price it pays, so its costs of supplying electricity have not risen significantly. Its request should therefore be denied.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the regulator's argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: A utility's request to raise its rates should be granted if the utility's costs of supplying electricity have risen significantly.
Long-term contracts at fixed prices are the most economical way for a utility to obtain electricity.
Increases in fuel prices raise the costs of companies that sell electricity to utilities under long-term contracts.
A utility's request to raise its rates should be granted only if the utility's costs of supplying electricity have risen significantly.
Most utilities that request permission to raise their rates cite increases in fuel prices.
questions.explanation: The regulator establishes that Dunmore's costs have not risen significantly and concludes the request should be denied, so the needed link makes rising costs a necessary condition for granting: grant → costs rose; costs didn't rise → deny. D supplies exactly that. A is the attractive trap: it makes rising costs sufficient for granting, which says nothing about what to do when costs have not risen.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Dunmore's rate request should be denied.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Dunmore buys all its power at fixed contract prices, so its costs haven't risen significantly.

breakdown.analysis: Costs haven't risen. So what? Why does that mean deny? We need a rule connecting 'costs not risen' to 'deny.' Chain: costs not risen → deny. Equivalently (contrapositive): grant → costs risen. In words: grant only if costs have risen. Watch for the reversal: 'grant if costs have risen' sounds identical but tells you nothing about a utility whose costs haven't risen. Here the needed link is a necessary condition, and the trap gives the sufficient version.

choices.note: Tempting: same words, wrong arrow. Costs risen → grant. Dunmore's costs didn't rise, so this rule is silent about Dunmore. It can't produce 'deny.'
Irrelevant. Whether fixed contracts are economical has nothing to do with whether this request should be denied.
If anything this hurts: it suggests Dunmore's suppliers might pass costs on eventually. It doesn't connect to denial.
CORRECT. Grant → costs risen. Contrapositive: costs not risen → don't grant. Dunmore's costs haven't risen, so the request should be denied.
What most utilities cite is irrelevant to whether this request should be denied.

questions.stimulus: Logistics manager: Six months ago our company began packing fragile goods in molded-pulp inserts instead of foam. In the six months since the switch, customers have filed 25 percent fewer damage claims for fragile goods than in the six months before. So the pulp inserts protect fragile goods better than the foam did.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the logistics manager's argument?
choices: Are molded-pulp inserts less expensive to purchase than foam inserts?
Do customers prefer receiving goods packed in molded pulp rather than in foam?
Have other shipping companies also switched from foam to molded-pulp inserts?
Are damage claims for fragile goods more common than damage claims for other goods?
Did the number of fragile goods the company shipped change substantially between the two six-month periods?
questions.explanation: Fewer claims means better protection only if the company shipped a comparable number of fragile goods in both periods; if shipments fell by a third, a 25 percent drop in claims would mean a higher damage rate. E asks exactly that. A raises a different dimension (cost), and D compares fragile goods with other goods rather than the two periods.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Pulp inserts protect fragile goods better than foam.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Damage claims for fragile goods fell 25 percent in the six months after the switch.

breakdown.analysis: Claims fell 25 percent. But out of how many shipments? If the company shipped half as many fragile items after the switch, a 25 percent drop in claims would actually mean more damage per shipment. A count only means something next to the volume. Good evaluate answers give you a different verdict depending on the answer: same volume → the argument looks good; big drop in volume → it falls apart.

choices.note: Wrong dimension: cost, not protection.
Customer preference isn't protection. Either answer leaves the argument where it was.
What other companies do tells us nothing about how well pulp protected this company's goods.
Wrong comparison. The argument compares two time periods for fragile goods, not fragile goods with other goods.
CORRECT. If volume held steady, fewer claims suggests better protection. If volume dropped a lot, the decline in claims could mean nothing, or even a worse damage rate.

questions.stimulus: Primatologist: Researchers have watched the gibbons of the Selan Reserve for more than two thousand hours and have never seen one use a tool, and some have concluded that Selan gibbons do not use tools. But this conclusion is unwarranted, since nearly all of those hours of observation took place in the high canopy during daylight. Thus, Selan gibbons probably do use tools, but only in places and at times when they have not been observed.
questions.stem: The primatologist's reasoning is flawed in that it
choices: treats the inadequacy of the evidence offered for a conclusion as grounds for accepting that the conclusion is probably false
draws a general conclusion about Selan gibbons from observations made only in the canopy during daylight
fails to consider that gibbons in other reserves might use tools in the places where they are observed
presumes, without providing justification, that researchers would recognize tool use by gibbons if they saw it
relies on the testimony of researchers whose expertise in gibbon behavior has not been established
questions.explanation: The primatologist correctly shows that the other researchers' evidence doesn't establish that the gibbons never use tools, but then concludes the gibbons probably do use tools, which nothing supports; A describes this. B is the attractive trap: it describes the flaw in the other researchers' reasoning, which the primatologist points out, not the primatologist's own mistake.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Selan gibbons probably use tools, just where and when no one has watched.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The no-tools conclusion rests on observation almost entirely in the canopy in daylight, so it's unwarranted.

breakdown.analysis: The first half is fine: limited observation can't prove the gibbons never use tools. But the primatologist then flips to 'they probably do.' Where's the evidence for that? There isn't any. Showing an argument is weak doesn't show its conclusion is false. It's like saying your proof that there's no milk in the fridge is bad because you only checked one shelf, so there's probably milk. You might think the flaw is the limited sample, but that's the opponents' flaw, which the primatologist catches. We need: undermining the evidence for X treated as evidence against X.

choices.note: CORRECT. Knocking down the 'no tools' evidence leaves us not knowing. The primatologist jumps to 'probably do,' which needs evidence of its own.
Tempting: this is a real flaw, but it's the other researchers' flaw. The primatologist is the one pointing it out. Read whose reasoning the stem asks about.
choices.example: Example of flaw: We watched only in daylight and saw no hunting, so these gibbons never hunt.

choices.note: Other reserves are irrelevant to the argument about Selan gibbons.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Gibbons elsewhere use tools, so Selan gibbons must too.

choices.note: The primatologist doesn't rely on this. If anything, doubting recognition would be another reason to distrust the 'no tools' conclusion, not a flaw in the primatologist's leap.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Observers saw no tool use, and observers always spot tool use, so there was none.

choices.note: The primatologist doesn't rely on anyone's testimony as an authority. The issue is the inference, not credentials.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A famous professor says gibbons use tools, so they do.

questions.stimulus: Preschool director: A child should be moved into the next age group's classroom ahead of schedule if the child's parents request the move and, in addition, either the child's current teacher recommends the move or the child scores well above the typical level on our readiness assessment.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated by the preschool director?
choices: Maya's teacher recommends moving her ahead, and Maya scored well above the typical level on the readiness assessment. So Maya should be moved ahead.
Theo's parents requested that he be moved ahead, but his teacher does not recommend the move. So Theo should not be moved ahead.

Priya's parents requested that she be moved ahead, and although her teacher has no opinion on the matter, Priya scored well above the typical level on the readiness assessment. So Priya should be moved ahead.
Lena scored well above the typical level on the readiness assessment, and her teacher has told her parents that she could be moved ahead. So Lena should be moved ahead.
Sam's parents requested that he be moved ahead, and Sam scored at the typical level on the readiness assessment. So Sam should be moved ahead.
questions.explanation: The principle requires a parental request plus at least one of two further conditions (teacher recommendation or a well-above-typical score); Priya meets the request and the score condition, so moving her ahead conforms (C). A satisfies both 'or' conditions but omits the required parental request, and B wrongly draws a 'should not' conclusion from a principle that only says when a child should be moved.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Parents request AND (teacher recommends OR score well above typical) → move child ahead.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: To justify 'move ahead': (1) parents requested it, and (2) teacher recommends it or the score is well above typical.

breakdown.analysis: Does each child pass every test? Two gates: the parental request is required, and then one of two others. The principle only tells you when to move a child; it never says when not to. So any 'should not' answer is suspect, and any 'should' answer must show the request plus one of the two.

choices.note: Tempting: both 'or' conditions are met. But we never hear that Maya's parents requested the move, and that part is required.
The principle says when a child should be moved, not when one shouldn't. Failing one route (teacher) doesn't trigger 'don't move', and Theo's score is unknown anyway.
CORRECT. Parents requested (required condition met), and the high score satisfies the 'or.' The teacher's lack of opinion doesn't matter since the score covers it.
The teacher said she could be moved ahead, which isn't a request by the parents. The required condition is left unknown.
Parents requested, but a typical score isn't 'well above typical,' and we don't know of any teacher recommendation. The 'or' is left unmet.

questions.stimulus: Every painting in the Ostrander collection is insured, as are about half of the sculptures in the collection. Some of the insured works in the collection are currently on loan to other museums. So some of the works now on loan are paintings, and some are sculptures.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Every trail in Harlan Park is maintained by volunteers, as are about half of the park's campgrounds. None of the areas maintained by volunteers is open in winter. So no trail in the park is open in winter, and neither is any campground that volunteers maintain.
Every sedan on Corbin's lot has a warranty, as do about half of the trucks on the lot. The vehicle that Ms. Avila bought from the lot has a warranty. So it must be either a sedan or a truck.
Most of the poems in the Brightwater anthology rhyme, and most of the poems in the anthology are sonnets. So at least some of the sonnets in the anthology rhyme.

All of the apprentices at the Renfrew bakery have taken the food-safety course, as have about half of the bakery's delivery drivers. Some of the employees who have taken the course work the night shift. So some night-shift employees are apprentices, and some are delivery drivers.
Every fern in the greenhouse needs daily misting, as do about half of the orchids. So about half of the plants in the greenhouse that need daily misting are orchids.
questions.explanation: The argument assumes that because both paintings and some sculptures fall into the insured group, and some insured works are on loan, the loaned works must include both kinds; but the insured works on loan could all be paintings, or all sculptures. D repeats this exact overlap error. B is tempting because it uses the same opening premise, but its flaw is overlooking other kinds of vehicles; C is a valid inference (two 'most' groups in one anthology must overlap), so it can't match a flawed argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Some loaned works are paintings and some are sculptures.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All paintings are insured; about half the sculptures are insured; some insured works are on loan.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are C; about half of B are C; some C are D; so some D are A and some D are B.

breakdown.analysis: Some insured works are on loan. Which ones? We aren't told. Picture it: the insured group contains paintings and some sculptures. 'Some insured works are on loan' could mean two paintings, or two sculptures. Nothing forces one of each. That's the overlap fallacy: knowing a group overlaps with two others doesn't tell you a subset of that group touches both. Find the answer with the same three premises and the same doubled conclusion.

choices.note: Valid. Volunteer-maintained → closed in winter. Trails and the volunteer-run campgrounds are volunteer-maintained, so they're closed. The conclusion follows, and a valid argument can't match a flawed one.
Tempting: same first premise. But the flaw is different: Ms. Avila's car could be some other warrantied vehicle, like a van. There's no 'some C are D' step and no split conclusion.
Valid. Two groups that each make up most of the same anthology must overlap. Good test of quantifiers, but it isn't flawed.

CORRECT. All apprentices took the course; about half the drivers did; some course-takers work nights; so some night workers are apprentices and some are drivers. The night-shift course-takers could all be apprentices, or all drivers. Same overlap error.
A different flaw: it confuses the share of orchids that need misting with the share of misted plants that are orchids (it depends on how many ferns and orchids there are). No 'some C are D' step.

questions.stimulus: Poetry critic: Late in his life, the poet Anselm Rook revised many of his early poems before including them in his collected works, and most readers today know those poems only in their revised versions. Scholars who want to understand how Rook's style developed over his career should therefore study the versions of the early poems that were first published, rather than the revised versions.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the poetry critic's argument depends?
choices: The versions of Rook's early poems that were first published are of higher literary quality than the revised versions.
At least some of Rook's revisions changed stylistic features of the poems he revised.
Rook revised his early poems many years after they were first published.
Most readers of Rook's collected works are unaware that the early poems were revised.
Rook's style changed more during the early part of his career than at any later point.
questions.explanation: The recommendation to study the original versions makes sense only if the revisions altered the style in some way; if no revision changed any stylistic feature, the revised versions would reveal Rook's early style just as well, so B is required. C is the attractive trap: the stimulus says the revisions came late in life, but the argument doesn't depend on any particular gap in time, only on the revisions' having changed the style.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Scholars tracing Rook's stylistic development should study the first-published versions of the early poems, not the revisions.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Rook revised many early poems late in life; most readers know only the revised versions.

breakdown.analysis: Why avoid the revisions? Only because they might not show how Rook wrote back then. But what if the revisions only fixed typos and spelling, leaving every stylistic feature intact? Then the revised poems show the early style just fine, and there's no reason to prefer the originals for this purpose. We need: the revisions changed the style at least somewhat. Negate each choice and look for the one that breaks the argument.

choices.note: Quality isn't the issue. Scholars tracing style want the earliest record, better or worse.
choices.negation: The first-published versions are not of higher quality than the revisions. (The argument still works.)

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: no revision changed any stylistic feature. Then the revised versions show the early style as well as the originals, and the recommendation has no basis. Note the modest 'at least some.'
choices.negation: None of Rook's revisions changed any stylistic feature of the poems he revised.

choices.note: Tempting, since the stimulus says 'late in his life.' But negate it: the revisions came only a few years after publication. If they still changed the style, the originals remain the better record. The argument survives.
choices.negation: Rook did not revise his early poems many years after they were first published.

choices.note: About general readers, not scholars. The critic's advice doesn't depend on what readers know.
choices.negation: Most readers of the collected works are aware the early poems were revised. (No effect on the advice to scholars.)

choices.note: Unsupported ranking. Rook's style can have developed without its early changes being the biggest ones.
choices.negation: Rook's style did not change more early in his career than at any later point. (The argument still works.)

questions.stimulus: Economist: In the Halvik region, the price of firewood rose sharply last winter. Most households in Halvik heat their homes with natural gas, and early last winter the price of natural gas rose steeply. Facing higher gas bills, many of these households likely turned to wood stoves for heat, and the resulting increase in demand for firewood is what drove up its price.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the economist's argument?
choices: The price of natural gas in Halvik fell slightly near the end of last winter.
Some households in Halvik heat their homes with electricity rather than with natural gas or wood.
Last winter was colder in Halvik than any winter in the previous decade.
Firewood prices also rose sharply last winter in neighboring regions where few households heat with natural gas.
Last winter, Halvik households that heat mainly with natural gas burned considerably more firewood than in previous winters, while households that heat only with wood burned about the same amount.
questions.explanation: E confirms the proposed mechanism: the extra firewood demand came specifically from gas-heating households, while wood-only households, unaffected by gas prices, did not increase their use. C is tempting because a cold winter would raise demand for firewood, but that is a rival explanation that does not depend on gas prices, so it weakens the argument; D likewise points to a cause other than gas prices.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Higher gas prices drove gas-heating households to burn wood, and that demand raised firewood prices.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Gas prices rose steeply early in the winter; firewood prices rose sharply; most households heat with gas.

breakdown.analysis: Two prices rose in the same winter. Did one cause the other? The economist only says households 'likely' switched to wood. Maybe something else raised firewood prices: a cold snap, a poor harvest. We need evidence that the switching actually happened, ideally showing extra demand came from gas households specifically.

choices.note: A late-winter dip in gas prices doesn't help show why firewood prices rose. If anything it's irrelevant.
Electric heaters are a different group. Irrelevant to whether gas households drove up firewood demand.
Tempting: a cold winter does raise firewood demand. But that's a rival cause that works without any switch from gas. It weakens the argument.
Opposite. If firewood prices rose just as much where almost nobody uses gas, something other than gas prices was probably at work.
CORRECT. The extra wood burning came from gas households, and wood-only households, unaffected by gas prices, didn't increase. That's the mechanism the economist proposed.

questions.stimulus: A survey asked every parent of a child between the ages of three and six in the town of Brell to compare the amount of time their own child spends on screens with the amounts spent by the other surveyed parents' children. Each surveyed parent has exactly one child in that age range. Most of the parents said they believe their own child spends less time on screens than do most of the other surveyed parents' children.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Not every surveyed parent who holds this belief about his or her child's screen time is correct.
Most of the surveyed parents are mistaken about how much time their own children spend on screens.
Surveyed parents tend to underestimate the amount of time their own children spend on screens.
Children between the ages of three and six in Brell spend less time on screens than do children of the same age elsewhere.
The surveyed parents whose children spend the most time on screens are the ones most likely to be mistaken.
questions.explanation: At most about half of the children can spend less screen time than most of the others, yet most parents believe their child does, so at least some of those parents must be wrong (A). B is the attractive trap: the arithmetic shows only that some believers are wrong, not that most parents are, and C goes further by assuming the errors come from underestimating rather than, say, overestimating other children's screen time.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Every Brell parent of a 3-to-6-year-old surveyed, one child each; 2. Most say their child has less screen time than most of the other children.

breakdown.analysis: Can most children be below most of the others? No. Line up 100 children by screen time. A child beats 'most of the others' only if it has less screen time than at least 50 of the other 99. At most 49 children can do that. But more than 50 parents believe their child does. So at least a couple of them are wrong. That's all that follows. Hard to prephrase the wording; watch for answers that stretch 'some are wrong' into 'most are wrong' or that guess at why they're wrong.

choices.note: CORRECT. Awkward double negative, but that's the point: 'not every believer is right' just means at least one is wrong, which the numbers force.

Tempting, and the classic trap. The numbers force only a few mistakes. If 55 parents believe it and 49 children qualify, as few as six are wrong. 'Some' isn't 'most.' It also shifts to absolute screen time when the survey asked about comparisons.
We don't know the direction of the error. A wrong parent might misjudge other children's screen time instead of their own child's.
Wrong comparison. The survey compared Brell children with each other, not with children elsewhere.
Plausible, but nothing in the survey tells us which parents are wrong. Unsupported.

questions.stimulus: Hospital administrator: Two years ago, our hospital began requiring that every medication order be double-checked by a pharmacist before the medication is given to a patient. Since then, the number of medication errors reported each year has fallen by 40 percent. So the double-check rule has substantially reduced the harm that medication errors cause our patients.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the administrator's argument?
choices: Since the rule took effect, the hospital has made it easier for staff to report medication errors.
Pharmacists at the hospital spend considerably more of their time checking orders than they did before the rule took effect.
The errors that pharmacists' checks catch are mostly minor discrepancies, while nearly all errors that seriously harm patients occur when medication is given rather than when it is ordered.
Medication errors are reported more often at hospitals that do not require pharmacists to double-check orders.
Several other hospitals in the region adopted similar double-check rules at about the same time.
questions.explanation: The evidence is a drop in the number of reported errors, but the conclusion is about harm; C shows that the errors the rule eliminates are mostly harmless while the harmful ones arise at a stage the rule does not touch, so the harm may not have fallen at all. A is tempting because reporting changes often undermine such arguments, but easier reporting would make a 40 percent drop even more impressive, strengthening the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The double-check rule has substantially reduced the harm medication errors cause.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the rule began, reported medication errors fell 40 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Is the number of errors really the measure of harm? One serious error can outweigh a hundred trivial ones. The evidence counts errors; the conclusion is about harm. If the rule only cuts trivial errors, harm could be unchanged. We need an answer that brings in severity: the errors that disappeared weren't the harmful ones.

choices.note: Tempting, because reporting changes are a familiar weakener. But read the direction: easier reporting should push reported errors up, so a 40 percent drop looks even more real. This strengthens.
Wrong dimension: the cost of the rule in staff time, not its effect on harm.
CORRECT. It splits errors by severity. The rule catches mostly minor errors at the ordering stage, while serious harm happens at administration, which the rule doesn't touch. Fewer errors, same harm.
This fits the administrator's story (no double-check, more errors). It doesn't weaken.
Irrelevant. Other hospitals' timing says nothing about whether this rule reduced harm here.

questions.stimulus: Of the soil samples taken from the Ardon test plots this year, every sample with a high clay content retained water well. None of the samples that retained water well came from plots that had been left fallow. Some of the samples from the plots treated with compost had a high clay content.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true of the soil samples taken from the Ardon test plots this year?
choices: Some of the samples that retained water well did not have a high clay content.
Every sample from the compost-treated plots came from plots that had been left fallow.
None of the samples from fallow plots had a high clay content.
Some of the samples from the compost-treated plots did not retain water well.
Every sample that retained water well came from the compost-treated plots.
questions.explanation: Chaining the facts: high clay → retains water → not fallow. Some compost samples had high clay, so some compost samples were not from fallow plots, which makes B impossible. C is the most tempting wrong answer because it looks unusual, but it actually must be true (any high-clay sample retained water and so was not from a fallow plot), and an answer that must be true can certainly be true.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. High clay → retains water; 2. Retains water → not fallow; 3. Some compost samples have high clay.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: high clay → retains water → not fallow. Fact 3 drops some compost samples into the start of the chain, so some compost samples retained water and were not fallow. Anything that contradicts that is the answer. Remember the CANNOT stem: the four wrong answers are all things that could be true (some even must be true).

choices.note: Could be true. The rule is high clay → retains water, not the reverse. Low-clay samples can retain water too.
CORRECT. Some compost samples had high clay, so they retained water, so they weren't from fallow plots. 'Every compost sample was from a fallow plot' contradicts that.
Tempting only because it sounds definite. In fact it must be true: high clay → retains water → not fallow. Contrapositive: fallow → not high clay. Something that must be true can be true.
Could be true. We know only that some compost samples had high clay. Others could have low clay and drain fast.
Could be true. Nothing rules out every water-retaining sample being from compost plots.

questions.stimulus: Art market analyst: Ten years ago, works by living artists accounted for 40 percent of the total value of the art sold at the Ferrand auction house. Last year, they accounted for only 25 percent. Clearly, collectors at Ferrand are spending less on works by living artists than they did a decade ago.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the analyst's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes that collectors at Ferrand are representative of art collectors in general
confuses the number of works by living artists sold at Ferrand with the total value of those works
takes for granted that works by living artists are generally less expensive than works by artists who have died
fails to consider that the total value of the art sold at Ferrand may have grown substantially over the decade
presumes, without providing justification, that the prices of individual works by living artists have fallen
questions.explanation: A smaller share of a larger total can be a larger amount: if Ferrand's total sales doubled, 25 percent of the new total would exceed 40 percent of the old. D names this overlooked possibility. B is tempting because it sounds like the classic number-versus-value error, but the analyst uses value consistently throughout; the confusion is between a share and an absolute amount.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ferrand collectors spend less on living artists' work than a decade ago.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Living artists' share of Ferrand's sales value fell from 40 percent to 25 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Their share fell. Did the dollars fall? Not necessarily. Say Ferrand sold $10 million ten years ago: 40 percent is $4 million. Last year it sold $30 million: 25 percent is $7.5 million. Smaller slice, bigger pie, more money. That's the percent-versus-amount flaw. Worth knowing cold. We need an answer that points out the total may have grown.

choices.note: The conclusion is only about Ferrand's collectors, so representativeness doesn't matter.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Ferrand's buyers prefer old masters, so collectors everywhere do.

choices.note: Tempting, since it sounds like the classic number/value mix-up. But the analyst talks about value in both the premises and the conclusion. The real shift is from share to amount.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Fewer living artists' works were sold this year, so collectors spent less on them.

choices.note: The argument never compares prices of living and dead artists' works.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Living artists' share is falling because their works are cheaper.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the total grew enough, 25 percent of it can be more money than 40 percent of the old total. A falling share doesn't mean falling spending.
The argument doesn't assume this; it concludes something about total spending, which could fall even if prices held. The flaw is the share-to-amount move.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Living artists' works sell for less now, so they must be less admired.
